A REGULAR BAD UN.

I. H. 'Yes, Sammy's a sad un, A change in the house, ma'am, A radical he; A sad un—you'll find; A regular bad un, All still as a mouse, ma'am; As ever you see. I'll draw up the blind. His riot and tearing No, no! I ain't fretting— And banging about HE doeth all well! Is really past bearing— But, as for forgetting— It's wearing me out. ' Ah, mothers can tell! And rambling and roaming. Yes, these is my riches, And larks in t be lane— My jewels and gold— Your cleaning and combing The jacket and breeches Is labour in vain. ` I made him of old. And as for his pinner— .I brush 'em and air 'em, It's ruin, I vow: And lay 'em out right. Clean on for his dinner— As though he would wear 'em And look at it now! 0' Saturday night. And scrubbing the tiles, rua'am,But no little Sammy And dusting the things. Comes runninganon, It ain't worth your whiles. A-calling out, "Mammy, ma'am, Just look at 'em on !' For mud as he brings. When the housework is ending, And growing, and poking Tow'rds three of the clock, His toes through his shoes! I still sit a-mending Without any joking Some little grey sock. We ought to be Jews. And sometimes—through Whatever's unlawful— thirsting Oil, blacking, or ink— And longing so sore— tell you it's awful I hear him come bursting The things as he'll drink. And banging the door. Then lost, and run over, And jump up to hold him, And choking, and fights— And feed on his smiles— My life ain't no clover Oh. how could I scold him A-getting such frights. For soiling the tiles! It's mischief and shindy All the gold ever minted Week. Sunday and all— I'd gladly give o'er That hole in the windy To see his foot printed Was him and his ball. In mud on the floor. And then there'shis dad, ma'am, There's the bed where I laid A-taking his part, him. And spoiling the lad, ma'am, My precious at night. With toffee and tart. And the quilt as I made him, No use now—not any— So cosy and light. A-climbing my knees! And now as he's lying And axing a penny! Down under the mould, Hear that, if you please! I'm waking and crying You're anus a-stuftin' A-thinklng he's cold. And spoiling your tea; I know as it's blindness-- No penny, you ruffin, Rebellious I am; No penny from me. The Shepherd in kindness It's a rod I'll be buying Has folded his lamb. I'm sober, I am ; But oh! how I miss him, I've set him off crying! And hunger to kiss him, Ah, mother's pet lamb l My own little Sam !: Look here now i what's this,lad? Then give me a kiss, lad— —Good Words, Rev. F. Leen. My own little Sam I bridge.

REMINISCENSES OF THE ROAD; os, DOWN ON ms LUCK. BY A GOEMIN. (Concluded from last week.) In my last article I concluded by Informing my readers nevi I came to enlist in the service of the cele- brated Dr. Squills (whose plain patronymic was Patrick O'Brien, from County Cork), in the humble capacity of bill sticker in ordinary. Carrying a paste tin. may not seem a very exciting pursuit, and the posting of small i placards may not be an occupation, n the opinion of many people, involving much risk, or one calling for great intellectual abilities. The work, however, gives an opportunity for the display of talent little imagined, especially if the bill sticker should be determined to cut' out all competitors. This was the laudable ambition which swelled my own bosom as I sallied forth to begin my new occupation. I Stuck bills seVerywbere. If I found a notice expressly forbidding me to do so, I planted a placard on the top of it; not forgetting "plinty av pashte.' I went on, and flourished. Every night I receiVed my daily pay of 25., after I had given a full account of how the bills and the paste had been die- posed' of. I worked that district thoroughly a pillar nor a post for miles round escaped my well-meant , intention; and shopkeepers, when opening their premises in the morning, were not infrequently sur- prised to find a row of my master's recommendations pasted across the shutters. Nemesis, however, was on my track, for one day, when, engaged in neatly decorating with bills the top of a tombstone which com- manded a good view of the road by which the grave- yard was situated, I was gently tapped on the shoulder by a stalwart guardian of the peace, and quietly informed that my energies were running into mis- directed channels, and that he could not allow me,, consistently with his duty to the public' no matter what might be his private inclination, to turn the sacred domains of the dead into a private posting station for My master, whatever might be the excellency of His wares. He was a gentle-voiced, smooth-tongued, but most inexorable bobby; and it was in vain that 1, appealed to his clemency. He Confiscated my paste and remaining stock of I bills, and delicately hinted to me that my presence before the justices would be urgently required in the morning, and that the more promptly to ensure my attendance, he was under the painful need- sity of accommodating me with a single bedroom at the police-station. Here was a pretty kettle of fish. My master got to hear of the circumstance by Some means; and after an interview he had with the authorities, I was set at liberty, and so disgusted was I with the cold and unsympathetic manner in which my energies had beeil rewarded that I shook the dust of the town from my feet, and departed without even going through the con- ventional ceremony of bidding adieu to the doctor. For a day or two• I wandered about the country un- certain what to do. A last driven by the stress of cir- cumstances to do somitihing I invested my entire stock of money (60.) in a pound of scented lozenges, and in spite of the authorities and the police took my stand in the ptiblic Market of a small border town and offered my wares—at 4d. an ounce! I had the gift of the gab and I used it freely to describe the unparalleled virtues of my pectoral Jujubes. I represented them to be made of the essences of herbs unknown to the ordinary botanist, and procured by my agents abroad—fancy !—at an enormous cost. I told the people that I was actuated. by no desire for gain, but by the hope of benefiting suffering humanity. The, lozenge's " took " almost as well as the almanacs did in the earlier part of my career as a tramp; and I kept to the business for a good whilc. One Saturday night I started off for my lodgingi, *bleb were two or three miles distant, with the prpceeds of my evening's Salea in my pocket, amounting to about 155., and my unsold wares in a box under my arm. The road was a lonely one, but it was lit with ldnips the entire distance. So ,far apart were they, however, that they were of little use as a means of protection against thieves. , I was trudging along, deeply occupied with my own , thoughts, when, between two of the lamps, and in the ;darkest and lonliest part of the road, I was set upon by three men. I THE INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION DEPUTATION TO AMERICA.—The arrangements for the presentation to the , President of the United States of the address which has been prepared by the International Arbitration Associa- tion are progressing favourably. The address will be presented by a deputation of English members of Parlia- ment. It has been signed by 230 English, Welsh, and Scotch members, but no Irish members have signed it. Mr. Bright has also written saying that he will watch the proceedings in the States with great interest. The arrangements for the interview with and introduction to President Cleveland will be made by Mr. Andrew Carnegie, who leaves England on October 8. ' Mr. SPURGEON ON THE SIGNS OF THE TIMES.-011 SlITI• day night Mr. Spurgeon preached to a vast congregation at the Metropolitan Tabernacle. The theme was the centurion's' appeal to Christ to "speak the word only" on behalf of his sick servant. After unfolding the sig- nificance of the narrative, Mr. Spurgeon proceeded to apply its lessons to the life of to-day. He said that he had had much rather gruesome talk of late with anxious friends about the signs of the times—and truly they were ominous enough—and he generally found that they wound up their remarks with words which implied that the darkness and disorder of the age was itself a witness to the early advent of the Son of Man. He yielded to no one in believing the second advent to be the brightest hope which shone in the skies of the Church; but he wished to impress on all to whom his influence could reach that we were called to do Christ's bidding now. Some men shook their heads, and said that the old truth was dying; but eyes enlightened by faith could see a great multitude of preachers yet unborn who should arise to proclaim it unshorn of its ancient simplicity and power. A PAUPER'S BURIAL: ANOTHER SRC/MIRO CASE.-i few days ago a man named William Sleaford, who had tramped from Manchester with his wife and three children, arrived in Bradford. The eldest child, a girl nine years of age, fell ill in the street, and died in her father's arms just as the family had entered the town. The body was taken to the mortuary, and on Friday a coffin, which had been made according to measurements taken by the workhouse undertaker, was also taken there for the reception of the body. The coffin was 2in. short, and was of such insufficient depth and width that when the body had been with great difficulty crushed into it, the shoulders were forced forward, and the arms had to be crossed over the body, and it was evident that the lid could not be pressed to within an inch of the sides. In response to the appeals of the distressed father the undertaker purchased some rough wooden ribs atan adjoining joiner's shop and hammered them on to the coffin whilst the body was in it. The pieces were too narrow, and the coffin was still too small, but the lid was fastened down with four screws, though the hands had to be crushed in the process, and one of the coffin sides split, In this condition the body was deposited in the grave.

Sinuous Guisrown-sn EXPLOSION AT WIGAN. --- Much damage -was done - on Saturday night by the ex- plosion of gunpowder in a house occupied by James Jones, collier, Spring-gardens, Wigan. Jones Ikept his stock of blasting powder, about 31bs., for use in the mine, in -a tin can in a cupboard underneath the stairs. Mrs. Jones having put her children to bed blew out the candle as slit was coming downstairs and went outside: A few minutes afterwards the neighbourhood was startled by a loud report, and smoke and flames issuing from Jones's house. Help was quickly rendered, the three children rescued, and the ,flaines subdued. It was tnen found that the powder had been ignited, most probably by the spark from the candle falling between the crevice of the stairs. . The blast seems to haN43 spent itself on the out- side walls, the cottage being a single one.

CoLLIERt ACCIDENTS.—Loss OF LIFE.— On Monday afternoon, whilst a shift of sinkers were fol- lowing their employment at .one of the Staveley Coal and Iron. Company's sinking pits, near to Markham, Bolsover, Chesterfield, the engineman allowed the skip to run with great velocity to the pulleys. The result was the breakage of timber and other substance, which fell a distance of, 450 yards into tbe shaft, killing G. T. Pressley, Alfred Smith, and Benjamin Glossop, all resi- alents of 13olsover district. Jackson. the engine-driver, bears a most excellent character, and much sympathy is felt for him. Another man died shortly; after admission to Chesterfield Hospital, where a fifth man is lying in a critical condition. Injuries were also sustained by other men working in the pit.—A shocking accident happened on Monday.at No. 4 Pit of the Griff Colliery, Warwick- shire. While a number of men were engaged in the workings there was a sudden fall of coal. A man named William Brooks was buried in the debris, and was shortly afterwards taken out dead, his injuries being of a fright- ful character. Another man, named Charles Reader, was so bully hurt that death ensued in a few minutes. Brooks leaves a widow and five children. TRADES UNION STATISTICS.-- The first report is- sued by the Board of Trade states • that it has been found possible to obtain particulars, more or lass complete, as to no fewer than eighteen societies, which are, no doubt, a small proportion of the total trade unions in the country, numbering 252 by the last return. but still a sufficient number to exhibit the general working; while the number of members amounts to 198,341, as compared with a total membership of 278,868 among 187 unions, making returns and a probable total membership of over 600,000 amoug all trade unions throughout the country. In some cases, where the mem- bership is also large, the amount of contributions for all purposes is as high as £3 pee head and upwards; while amounts of over £2 per head are also common. On an income of 30s. per week, or about £7B per annum, a contribution of £3 would amount to about 4 per cent., and on £2 Per week, or £lOO per, annum, it. would still be 3 per cent. In some cases they must pay a good deal more than 3 or 4 per cent, to provide against the chanoes of their life, and if there is to be saving at all in addition the net earning available for ex- penditure must be a good deal less than the gross. The percentage of unemployed runs up to veil, high figures Indeed, as much in one case as over 20 per cent., while figures between 5 and 10 per cent, are not uncommon; the percentage of sick ranges between 2 and 3 per cent., while there are higher figures, and the percentage of superannuated in the older societies tends to be over 2 per cent. FRENCH GOLD MEDAL AWARDED TO AN ENGLISH OuSE.—Claret will this year be superior in quality, on account of the unstinted ripening the grapes have received from a continuously hot sun, but the quantity will be some- what less than last year. Snob is the report et Messrs. W. and A. Gilbey, by far the largest importers of wine into this country, and vineyard cultivatore themselves to a cou- ' siderable extent. The elopes whereon the harvest of bunches for the wine press are gathered in the Medoc dis- triet, are at this time covered with peasants and peasants' • children all happily occupied in securing the crop and carrying it to the aine-making premises. A description of the prosperous district is rich in charm, but it is impossible to iMproraour own agricultural position by imitation of the methods of our French neighbours. We have gravelly soils /bounding in loose stones to keep the land warm at night, but we have not sufficient sunshine to ripen grapes to any profit. Messrs W. and A. Gilbev have this year been awarded the French Ministerial gold medal for vine-grow- ing, so that, apparently, Englishmen are not prevented from practising viticulture abroad successfully.---.' Leeds Mer- cury," October 4th, 1887. FAILURE OF THE PROSECUTION AGAINST THE LORD MAYOR OF DUBLIN.—The summonses issued against Mr T D Sullivan, M.P., proprietor of the "Nation" newspaper, and Mr William O'Brien, M.P., editor of " United Ireland," for publishing reports of a meeting of a suppressed branch of the National League, contrary to the provisions of the Crimes Act, came on on Thursday before Mr O'Donel, chief police magistrate for Dublin. Mr Sullivan is Lord Mayor of Dublin, and in accordance with a resolution passed by the Nationalist majority of the City Council on Wednesday he appeared in court "in state," attended by sword and mace bearers, and accompanied by his colleagues in the Council. Mr O'Brien was not present. The Na- tionalist members of the Municipal Council had had seats allotted to them, to which they proceeded at once in quietness. But a great contention arose as to the accommodating of the " state" officials of the Lord Mayor, and it led to such a scene as has rarely been witnessed in a court of jestice. Mr. Sullivan's friends insisted that the sword and mace should be laid on the table in front of the bench. This the officers of the court would not permit, and for a time there was a struggle at the bar between them and the gentlemen contending for the due honouring of the in- signia of Mr. Sullivan's high office. The shouts and yells of the aldermen and councilmen in the gallery added to the excitement, which was only terminated by Mr. Sullivan proposing, and the court officials agreeing, that the sword and mace bearers regalia and all—should be accommodated in front of the gallery. After counsel for the Crown had stated the case against Mr. Sullivan, Mr. Healy, M.P., • the de- fendants' counsel, took several technical objections, and Mr. O'Donel held one of these objections to be fatal to the prosecution. The learned magistrate said he was struck at the close of the case for the prosecution by the fact that no evidence had been given that the alleged meeting was a meeting of the condemned association. There was, in fact, no proof that there had been any meeting at all of the mem- bers of the association, and he must dismiss the summons. On the application of counsel on both sides, Mr. O'Donel , consented to state a ease for the superior courts. 'llia 'charge against Mr. O'Brien was postponed.

A great number of the tenantry of North Cork have served originating notices to seek for a readjustment of their rents under -the new Irish Land Act. Monsignor Persico, the Papal Envoy., returns to Dublin in a week. 11e is expected to remain m the metropolitan city for about ten days, proceeding thence ta Rome. The total number of '^aseholders and judicial tenants who lodged fair rent claims under the new Land Act, up to the 28th of September was 15,877. Of these 9,856 are leaseholders, whose rents now come under review for the first time by lodging applications before Septem- ber 29th. The new rents will run from that date. The applications -E-,eived on September 28th numbered 8,511. At the Thuries Petty Sessions a young man named Richard Buckly has been committed for trial, charged with the abduction•of a girl named Power, between-15 and 18. She is the daughter of a farmer, and will be ,entitled to a considerable sum of money when of age. The prisoner, who is about 22, belongs to the labouring class. After his arrest he wrote to the girl's parents • offering to marry her, but the offer was refused. Sir &Minot Baker, in a letter slys :—As the Irish police are to occupy the position of "Aunt Sally" in the de- servedlY popular national game of cockshy, allow me to suggest to the authorities that the faces and heads of thiar figures would last longer without repairs if the police were provided with shields, instead of being ex- posed unprotected to a shower of stones and other missiles. A circular shield, two feet in diameter, of strong wicker-work covered with raw hide, would cost three shillings, and would thoroughly protect the police- man. This may be too simple an arrangement to, be ap- preciated by the heads of a department,•but it would save the heads of the constables, and would mitigate the exasperation which induces wounded Men ti resort to firearms.

More painful scenes occurred at Gweedore, on Wednes- day, on the evictions being resumed. A hundred police were present—fifty artted•with rifles, and fifty with batons. Boiling water was thrown over the sheriff's men, and in the result the tenants only capitulated at the inAigation of the parish priest.

THE LORD MAYOR .OF DUBLIN SUMMONED. The prosecution of the Lord Mayor and Mr. O'Brien, for publishing reports of the meetings of the suppressed branches of the National League has caused surprise and excitement. 2itte Preemies .Journal appeals to the judge ment of the cfillised world upon it as an iniquity, urging that the defendants have done their utmost, in conjunc- tion with all the Irish leaders, to restrain the people within the limits of constitutional action, and feels sure that in England the action of the Government will ex- cite a revulsion of feeling as great as the indignation necessarily created in Ireland. The Daily Express hails the renewed action of the Government as showing that no faltering will be found in them, and, believing that the Nationalist movement will collapse like an airbag under right treatment, declares that there must be no relaxation of 'energy at any point, Lid condonation of offences when the offender enjoys a position warranting the belief that he is a potent source of mischief. It is expected that the Solicitor-General, Mr. John Atkinson, Q.C., and Mr. Carson. will conduct the prosecution, and that Mr. D. B. Sullivan, Mr. T. M. Healy-, M.P., and Mr. Timothy Harrington, M.P., will be for the defendants. THE OUTRAGE BY EMERGENCY MEN.

The inquest on the body of John 7 Kinsella, who was killed in an encounter with emergency man at Cloghan, was resumed at Rallyfad on Monday. Inspector Rodwell appeared for the Crown.—Mr. Sullivan, representing the next-of-kin of the deceased, at the commencement of the proceedings expressed surprise that after the evidence of Friday against Freeman he should still be allowed at large. Michael Kavanagh, further examined, said no stones were thrown by the crowd in the yard, nor was any shot fired from the yard. Cross-examined, witness admitted that the people were drtermined to defend their cattle against seizure, warrant .or no warrant, but did not- strike the emergency men. Kinselys pushed Johnston back from the gate with a fork. Dr. Mouillot deposed to tracing in the body of the deceased a circular wound on the right side one inch from the breast bone. There was no other wound. The bullet passed between the third and fourth ribs, and lodged in the spinal canal. The right cavity of the lungs was full of blood Death must have been instantaneous. He identified the bUllet produced. • Dr. Metge, of Coolgreaney, corroborated, and deposed to being called in at nine o'clock at night to attend Scott, an emergency man, at Ballyfad.—Cross-examined, he said Scott's wound was very slight. ' Myles Kinsella said he heard the words "Fire, boys," but "did not see the first shot fired. His fathetfell down across his knees when shot. Be saw no stones thrown, and no firearms among the people in the Yard. , Stephen Maher gtated lie was inside this gate when a party of about 22 iti,number came up. Mc.Cabe, an emergency man, asked for Kavanagh, and said he had a Warrant to distrain against him for £57. Witnesses con- firmed the evidence of Michael Kavanagh reported on Friday. He saw Freeman with a revolver, and heard him exclaim he would shoot Kinsella. Deceased had a pitchfork in his right hand, and with his left pushed back Johnston. He saw Mc.Cabe level a rifle at him, and heard the shot, but was not struck Deceased was killed either by Freeman or Mc.Cabe. He heard two volleys fired and the word, "Fire. hoys.l The inquest was adjourned. THE ,SUPPRESSED LEAGUE. - - -

Several branches of the National League in the Mit- chelstown district held meetings on Sunday, despite the activity ,of a large force of police, who patrolled every locality.' At Mitchelstown prominent members of the League were followed by constables, who also visited Finns Fort and several barricaded houses, without, how- ever, dlsturbing any meeting. Several hundred per- sons eluded the police, and went to a fortified house just outside the town, where a meeting was held, over which Mr. John Mandevjlle, ' Mr. O'Brien's co-defendant, pre- Wed. In the course of his speech Mr. Mandeville said it was an impossibility to destroy the League. Letters were read from the Lord Mayor of Dublin (Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P.) and some Englishmen, asking to be elected members of the Mitchelstown branch. While the meeting was being held police patrols passed by the fortified house, but did not go in. At Shrabarla au; con- stables came upon a meeting just as. it-was dispersing, and Cautioned the members as to the illegality of their action. div.head: MR. BRUNNER, 'M.P., AT ASHTON.
div.p: MR. BRUNNER, 'M.P., AT ASHTON.

A ' crowded meeting in connection with the Ashton-Under-Lyne Liberal Association was held, on Monday night in the Ashton Town Hall. The chair was taken by Mr. Arthur E. Reyner, who was sup- ported amongst others by Mr. John T. Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich 41v18i0n of Cheshire, the Rev. Thomas Green, M.A., Mr. J. Hanna, Mr. J. W. Summers, Mr. J. D. Hibbert, Mr. S. H.. Emmett, Mr. A. Buckley, Mr. A. W. Rowley, and Dr. Cooke. In his opening remarks the Chairman emphatically denied tliat the Liberal party of this country were In favour of lawlessness, the degradation of the House of Commons, or the disintegration of the Empire. What they...desired, and what they believed their policy tended to, was the removal of just grievances in Ireland, and the creation of a lasting friendship between England and the sister country. Mr. Hanna submitted the following resolution :—" That this meeting desires to express its disapproval of the policy Of Her Majesty's Government in interfering with the rights of public meeting in Ireland, and it strongly condemns the conduct of the Government in attempting to justify the action of the police at Mitchelstown in firing upon unarmed people." This was seconded by Mr. S. H. Emmett, who took occasion to point out that the Liberal electors of Ashton are at the present time misrepresented in Parliament. They were, be said, told plainly at the general election that Mr. Addison was going to Parliament to represent the people on these lines—that there should be the same law in Ireland that there was in England. Yet what did they find? That the Government which dared not trust its police in the city of London with revolvers in order to meet men who were armed in their burglarious enterprises, yet armed the police in Ireland, and put them in a position to exerciee their revenge upon people who might have taken them unawares and turn their tail to the enemy when they expect to win the day. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner, M.P., on rising to support the resolution was received with great enthusiasm. He was very thank- ful, he said, to believe that the heart of Ashton was sound, and he would like them to know that the heart of Birmieg- barn was sound. On Friday night last be had a similar re- ception to that which he had just received. It was only the accident of his being a witness of the painful incidents at Mitchelstown, and no merits of his own, that had pro- cured him the honour of being invited to so many places. It was because he had told the truth about Mitcheletown that his countrymen paid him honour ; and five thousand people at Birmingham on Friday night last, against Mr. Chamberlain's will, did him the honour to rise as those now before him had done, aye, and three times over. (Cheers.) Mr. John Morley spoke on Saturday night of Mr. Chamber- lain's great power. He (Mr. Brunner) believed that Mr. Brunner was an exhanated volcano. (Laughter and cheers.) Two years ago, he allewed, Mr. Chamberlain was a great power in England. But why ? For this reason, and this alone, that when they heard him he appeared to them to them to have a heart full of sympathy for the poor, full of generosity for the suffering. Where was his generosity, where was his sympathy today? Mr. Chamberlain spoke of a man whom they all honoured, Sir Georee Trevelyan, as "crawling beck to the party." What was Mr. Cham- herlain's position ? His position! He had not one, but a dozen positions. He was gyrating and pirouetting, and swinging a shillelagh, and bitting at every Liberal's bead he saw. (Cheers,) With regard to local affairs, Mr.Brunner confessed that his visit to Ashton was made with the object of persuading the people te change their representation. He , had no personal quarrel with Mr. Addison; he was the jol- liest coercionist of them all. (Laughter., So jolly was he that he was always known as the .4 Ashton cherub." (Lend laughter and cheers.) He could assure them that they were not going to have a chance of altering the re- presentation until the next general election. Take his word for this—Mr. Addison was not going to be made a judge. (Laughter.) He would be uncommonly pleased to see Mr. Addison so honoured, and for this reason—the

MURDER OF A VIC?_111, BY HIS CURATE. •••-.2%. HORRIBLE TRAGEDY. A fearful murder was committed at midnight, on Saturday, at the vicarage of Cretingham, a small village near Framlingham, Suffolk. The vicar, the Rev. William yeynott Farley, aged 73, suffered from partial paralysis, a year ago engaged as a curate a clergyman known as the Rev. Mr. Gilbert Cooper, but who is also said to have given another name. The curate had resided with the vicar and Mrs. Farley, and for a ' few days had complained of sleeplessness. On Saturday night Mrs. Farley offere,l to read him to sleep, but 'ids offer he declined, saying that the noise of her reading to the vicar jarred upon his nerves. All the household had retired to rest, when about midnight Mrs. Farley heard a knocking at the door of 'the bedroom occupied by herself and the vicar. Mrs. Farley asked, " What is that?" and on un- locking the door she saw the curate in his dressing gown with a candlestick in his hand. He was quiet. but deadly pale, and in reply to her question as to what he wanted, tried to fovea his way in. With some difficulty she turned the key, exclaiming to her* husband, "Why, he is mad." Mr. Cooper called out, "I want to come in and see the vicar." Mr. Farley replied. "Oh, poor fellow, open-the door and see what he wants." She then admitt,ed him, but did not notice any-weapon in his hand. He walked direct to the bedside and put his left hand in the direction of the vicar's throat. Mr. Farley exclaimed, "What do you mean?" The curate laughed, turned 'round, and walked quietly out of the room. Before he reached the door Mr. Parley exclaimed in a weak voice," He has cut my throat." Mrs. Farley at first thought 'her husband delirious,and as she could see no blood replied. "Nonsense." She, however, followed Cooper and asked what he had in his hand. He replied "Nothing," and even then she could see no weapon. On going back she found Mr. Farley on the floor with blood rushing from his throat. She ran back to the curate and asked him to come and help, but he made no reply. She then des- patched the groom for the doctor, hut long before the latter arrived Mr. Farley was dead. After committing the deed, Mr. Gilbert Cooper left the yicarase, but returned about five o'clock on Sunday morning, wren he was taken into custody by a policeman who then had charge of the vicarage. He was removed to Framlingham Police sta- tion, and when questioned by the parish clerk he said he first thought of doing it on the previous day. The murdered clergyman had a grown up family, one of his sons being a doctor in London. Cooper came from Tunbridge Wells, but nothing is known of his family in the neighbourhood of Framlingham. Ile undertook the whole of the clerical duties of , the parish, but does not appear to have gained the affections of the parishioners. He was generally credited with High Church proclivities, . whereas the vicar was an Evangelical. There does not, however, seem to have been any quarrel or dispute be- tween the vicar and curate. On the contrary, circum- stances seem to show t hat very blindly relations existed between Mr. Cooper and Mr. and Mrs. Farley. ' INQUEST AND VERDICT.—CURIOUS EVIDENCE. Arthur Edward Gilbert Cooper, clerk in holy orders, was broughl up in custody, at Framlingham, on Mon- day, charged with the wilful murder of the Rev. Wm. Meymott Farley, at Cretingliam, on Sunday morning. The prisoner, when brought into court, refused to enter the dock, and when the was formally charged, lie said. in a low tone of voice, "Isn't he alive?' Superintendent Balls gave formal evidence, and the prisoner, when Asked if he had anything to say why he should not be remanded, replied, "I don t think there is any charge made out. lam not aware that Mr. Farley is dead. I don't believe he is." The prisoner was then remanded until Thursday, and was subsequently con- veyed to Cretinghatfi, to attend the coroner's inquest. The jury of farmers and tradesmen, having been sworn, proceeded to the vicarage to view the body, • which was lying in the bedroom where the tragedy oo- curred. The terrible gash on the throat was exposed and bloodstains on the carpet pointed out. The jury next proceeded to the curate's room, the bed in which was much disarranged, as if the occupant had been tossing from side to side. On the return to the Bell Inn the prisoner was brought in between two policemen, I and provided with a chair. fle seemed a man about 33 or 34 years of age. He kept on his hat until it was re- moved by one of the offi :tors. At first he was bewildered, but soon settled into close attention to what was going on, and teemed to appreciate ,the gravity of the situa- tion. The widow was the first witness. She thought the deceased was a man of 73. She is still in the prime of , life, having been his third wife. She was wonderfully ' calm, and still wore coloured flowers in her bonnet. She repeated the statement as to the manner in which the crime was perpetrated. Having tiniShed this recital, she said when the prisoner returned to the house she went up to see him.

div.p: TIM Resolutions passed at the meeting of the burgesses and inhabitants on Tuesday week with regard to the freeing of the War- rington Library came before the Town Coun- cil on Tuesday last; but they were not dis- cussed. The MAYOR engaged at the public Meeting, when the resolutions were adopted, that he would see that they were properly considered. But on Tuesday he insisted on their being referred, in the first instance, to the Library and Museum Committee. It would seem that he was misunderstood by those Who concluded that he intended the resolu- tions to be "properly considered " at the next Council meeting. There was an evident disposition on the part of various Aldermen and Councillors to ventilate the matter; but the MAYOR ruled that any discussion would be irregular until the question had been be- fore the Committee. On His WORSHIP being reminded that the matter had already. been before the Committee, he replied that it was " quite informal." It is puzzling, however, to see how he could arrive at such a conclu- sion, seeing that the meeting of the Library Committee was called together specially to consider the resolutions passed at the Town's Ueeting. The odd part of the thing is that Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, a leading member of the Library Committee, had urged that "it is not a Committee question, but one that Must be considered by the Town Council." It Is obvious that the art of circumlocution is not a lost art, and that there are people Yet in the world who have great faith in a Policy of masterly inactivity. There can be no question that it was within the province of the Town Council—as Alderman SUTTON Put it—to discuss the resolutions and ex- change opinions without coming to any de- finite resolution. It has been done a hundred times in a hundred towns upon what are known as " Mayor's communications." The Council could have gone further they Could, as Councillor H. ROBERTS sug gested, have discussed the matter by suspend- ing the Standing Orders; or they could, under the Standing Orders, have resolved themselves into a committee with a view to considering what should be done. Curiously enough, although so much anxiety was ex- pressed to proce 'd in a regular manner, the resolutions were, apparently, disposed of in an irregular fashion. It is understood that they are to be referred to the Library and Museum Committee, but no motion was submitted to the Council. Technically, the resolutions are still before the Town Council. The tame course was taken with the memorial a, s to the Howley intercepting depot; it was remarked that it would be re- ferred to the Sanitary Committee ; but there was no motion upon the subject. These enforced delays would, of course, be 0f small moment if it were not that there is ri uneasy feeling abroad that certain mem- bers of the Town Council are disposed to Make light of the wishes of the ratepayers; ?r at any rate stave off the consideration of their grievances until it is too late to seek ...iremedy by means of the annual elections. we shall be glad to find that there is no ground for this apprehension. There is to be a,nother meeting of the Town Council before 'he month is out; and if satisfactory con- clusions are not at that meeting come to, the , ratepayers will know that it rests with them to 11) ake their views felt by means of the ballot- Ox on the first of November. Meantime, hey Must be on the alert; they must watch 1 -vents, and prepare to control them.

Facts of this kind ought to -.try a world of argument with them. Our letrimercial travellers are active enough at °lne ; and it is a recognised rule with enter- rrising firms that the greater the number of iavellers the greater the business. But it ;4 a rule which holds good abroad as well -ha at home; and it is because we are paying due attention to it that e are left behind in the race. In England kere is no systematic training of a corn- such as we find in the special

We have what are called private R:rbrnercial schools; but compared with the t business schools of the Continent they ta,aS chalk is to cheese. Men who have Cue money in this country, and who are elllselves lacking in culture, have a fancy for Ing their sons "gentlemen," and to this they give them a classical education t:eh is more of ornament than of use to • Even tradesmen's sons, who should hq,',rained to follow and develop their fathers' "nesses, are stuffed with classics in 4eilv,a3r that is the reverse of beni- td,,'4l to them in after life. A "polite hitl'e4tion" is well enough in its way.; but in caqes out of ten one might say of the re- Rubbish shot here." In England is, unhappily, a great gap between elementary school and the college tkhgalo which needs filling by provision for Net education, and for such purely corn- eial schools as have been in existence on ve,.`-'entinent for a generation. We make lite Provision for drinking, but quite too, h'° thinking. Even when a good library ting.,c'tks has been got together, as at War- the authorities foolishly deny proper Iverv-sa to them, as though the inhabitants O barbarous that they would light their la it, Instead of their minds with them. div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
- - - - Lord Dunraven ventilated the Fair Trade erne at the Warrington Public Hill last night; it seems he has not yet done ravin'.

It is nice to be a President; but think of shaking hands with 9000 persons, as Presi- dent Cleveland did the other day at St. Louis. We shall have to add to Shakespeare after this fashion : Uneasy lies the head that wears the crown; But oh, what pains the President endures ho suffers shake of hand nine thousand times.

The inquiry into the circumstances of the death of the three men killed at Mitchelstown shows that there has been some hard swearing amongst the police. It begins to be demon- strated that the account of the Encrlish mem- bers of Parliament was true and straight, and that of the official statement was, to put it mildly, " slantingdicular."

The overseers for Appleton township seem to have got into an awful muddle with regard to the list of voters which they, or the assis- tant overseer, had prepared. It is a serious thing when a Revising Barrister has to re- mark that about 40 persons ran the risk of being disfranchised. The ratepayers ought to see if they cannot disfranchise the over- seers, or at any rate, give them the sack.

The Tories are not made hapov by the Hughes-Hallett scandal; and one of their journals gives the Colonel to understand that the best thing he can do is to speedily resign his seat for Rochester. On this issue the Liberals can join hands with the Conserva- tives—particularly as they will have a chance of winning in a contest. Any how, Colonel Hughes-Hallett's seat is looked upon as better than his company. The Newton Commissioners do not seem to be in any hurry to close with the offer of Mr. Lcgh to give ten acres of land for the purposes of a Park or Recreation Ground for Earlestown. It will, of course, cost some- thing to lay the land out; but if they cannot spare much they need not spend much They ought not to let the opportunity slip; the time may come when the land will be looked upon as a god-send.

Mr. Gladstone is more sympathetic than Mr. Bright as to the question of the payment of members of Parliament. He says : "Though I do not at present see any way to an arrangement, I cannot feel well satisfied with a state of things in which gentlemen of high birth or station receive pensions (acertain number) for pubic service, on the ground of insufficient means, and members of Parlia- ment elected by labouring men have to be re- turned or supported by contributions out of their daily wages."

Lord Ailesbury has been expelled by the Jockey Club for malpractices of a most dis- graceful kind; and even the Tory press seems to think there is something curiously wrong when such on offender is still good enough for the House of Lords. It is stated that his lordship, lapsing for a moment into sense, was on one occasion heard to exclaim— " Aint it strange that such a blessed fool as I am should be a lord ?" To use the language of the noble lord, one may say—"lt are strange," so strange as to shock the common sense of humanity. The Tories propose to tinker the House of Lords; but it is beyond repair ; it should be ended rather than mended.

Aldermen are a sot of House of Lords in our local Parliaments; they are elected after a fashion, but not by the ratepayers, and, holding office for six years, they are apt to forget that they owe any regard to the ratepayers. Besides, it usually happens Ithat they are made in batches by °Re political section, and from one political party. This is one way of forcing politics into Town Councils, and is as bad in its effects as bad can be. We require to reform this, and reform i it altogether.

Mr. Gladstone has made it clear more than once that he does not like Liberals to be spoken of as Glaclstonians. He remarked to a deputation at Harwarden Castle the other da.y that "he could not conceive how such an enormous power as the Liberal party possessed, and such •a great and far- reaching policy as they led, could construct itself into a mere personal name." Let politicians take the hint; Liberals, if you please, but not Gladstonians.

Mr. R. A. Naylor's memory seems to have failed him as to what he said on a certain Sunday, to his Thelwall congregation, about the honour that was conferred upon him by being permitted to speak to a meeting addressed by a real live lord. Our informant has, however, a distinct recollection of the incident; and suggests that Mr. Naylor may be expected next, as Byron has it, to "wear hi head denying that he wears it." As to the other incident referred to, it is ether ancient history, or Mr. Naylor must be dreaming.

A young man who is described as "res- pectable looking" has been fined los. and costs, and branded as a "rogue and vaga- bond" for carrying on a lottery on Widnes , Market Ground. The law is the law, of coarse; but we want it to catch big fish as well as little ones. There is the "respectable looking" churchwarden, or magistrate, who takes part in lotteries at bazaars. He breaks the same law as the young man who stands in the market; and people who like to see fair play want to know when he will be put in the dock and dealt with as a "rogue and vagabond." Professor 'Williamson, of Owens College, gives farmers to understand that they are too sparing of manure. Extra manuring is, he says, the secret of the success of Lothian far- mers. We have an instance nearer home of what manure can do. Councillor Bolton, of Warrington, has piled Ossa upon Pelion in the way of manure in his garden at Stock- ton Heath, and, blessed result, that manure has been converted in Nature's laboratory into apples weighing three quarters of a pound each, and into tomatoes nearly as heavy. The moral is not "line upon line," this time, but load upon load.

The member for Newton has furnished details of his adventure with brigands, from which it appears that the whole affair was of a much more prosaic character than was first supposed. He was never really in the hands of the brigands, havinz, when his followers came in contact with them, taken up what he calls '• a strategic position behind a bush." In other words, he hid himself while the gendarmes who were with him got him off scot free, on the ground that he was not only an Englishman, but an English agent. It is a pity he was not photogriphed as he ap- peared "behind a bush." We are quite sure his constituents would gladly have purchased copie3.

•I M The thoughtless off-hand way in which policemen sometimes give evidence has been curiously illustrated at Marylebone Police Coutt. A woman who was about to give evidence in a case of assault was taken pos- session of by a police constable,who proceeded to gorge her with having been drunk and incapable on the previous day. Ic was in vain that she protested ; the constable was cock-sure, and went on with the evidence. Eventually, it was found that he had got hold of the wrong woman ; and he has since had a bad half hour with his chief. He ought to be dismissed ; a constable who could make such a blunder wh:tn there was no suggestion of resemblance between the women is not fit to be in the force.

For some time past she bad suf- fered severely from heart disease and bad been under the care of a doctor. The coroner deemed an invest unnecee- eery. FUNERAL OF THE Rtrwconw SaxroN. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—The sudden death of Jas. Pickthall, aged 64, who resided at 40, Vine-street, Widnes, is reported. He had suffered from pains in the chest and the region of the heart, and up to a week before his death was under the medical treatment of Dr. McCambridge. He was c3mpelled to leave his work on t aturday and shortly after his return horns ha died. N 3 inquest was held.

STRANGE DEATH AT WIDNES.—The Sudden death of Thomas Hughes, 49 years of age, builder, of Deacon-road, is reported. On Thursday. Mr. Hughes followed his usual avocations, and in the evening, being a class leader at Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel, went to a meeting at that place. During the proceedings he was seized with a fit, and was conveyed home as soon as possible. Medical aid was summoned. but death ensued at three o'clock yesterday morning. TisAP AeCIDENT AT WlDNEs.—About Seven o'clock on Thursday evening, Mr Rhodes, butcher, Mersey-road, accom- panied by his wife, was driving along Dittou-road, when the shafts of the vehicle smashed, and the horse dashed away at a great speed. The occupants were thrown into the road, and the mutton, with which the conveyance was laden, was strewn beside them. Happily neither Mr. nor Mrs. Rhodes were seriously injured. The horse was not captured until it had got into Newtown. PILES are cured by Howell's Golden Herb Pills, of all Medicine Vendors.—Advt CONSERVATIVE CLUB FOR RUNCORN. A number of Conservatives met in the Public Hall the other evening with the object of forming a Conservative Club in Runcorn. Mr. J. Brundrit, occupied the chair. A committee, Coniiiiiting of Messrs. J. W. Lightburn, J. K. Digges, A. Jor- dan, W. Hankinson, W. H. Rogerson, Kilcross, Hough, J. J. W. Potter, T. Kirkham, Mitchell, and Sutton was ap- pointed to deal with the matter, with Mr. T. H. An.. nett as secretary. Lord Egert in had forwarded a cheque for £5. .

A LIBERAL CLUB FOR WIDNES.—On Thursday evening meeting of Widnes Liberals was held in Lacey-street School-reom with the object of considering the advisability of forming a Liberal club iu the town. Mr F. Hayes oc- cupied the chair, and there was a capital attendance. The meeting displayed great unanimity upon the subject, and it was ultimately decided to form a Working-men's Liberal Club. A ;-irovisioaal committee was appointed to carry out the scheme. It is intended that the funds of the insti- tution shall be raised by subscriptions, and it is desired that when formed the club shall be self-supporting. THE WIDNES INTERWORHS FOOTBALL COMPETITION.— The members of Messrs Sullivan and Co.'s football team, who stscceeded in winning the gold medals in the inter- works football competitien, gathered in the office of the works on Thursday afternoon. They were met by Mr J Brock, J.P., the managing director of the firm, and Mrs Brock, and the lady graciously presented each player with his gold medal. Mrs Brock afterwards made an apprepriate speech, and Mr Brock promised to entertain the team to d;nner at the Central Hoti-1 on Tuesday evening next. It will be remembered that Sallivan's team, after playing four undecided games with Messrs Oaken Deacon's team, van- quished them on the fifth meeting by 16 points to one; and thoroughly deserved their success. inwE WILL RETURN the purchase money if one box of Howell's Golden Herb Pile does not cure vou.—Advt. . .

SERIOUS ACCIDENT NEAR WIDNES —On Saturday night a serious accident occnried at Ditten Junction, near Wid- nes, to a young man named James Haan. It appears Hagan was a passenger by the 11 o'clock p m. train from Lime-street, Liverpool, to Runcorn, on the London and North-Western Railway, and bad booked for Widnes. On arrival at Ditton Junction he did not change as he shdeld have done, and he jumped out of the c+rritge whilst it was in motion. He lay unconscious for about ten minutes on the line, and afterwards he crawled to the water column, near Ditton Junction, where he was found by a man named Edward Martin. The injured man was conveyed home by Police-constable Worthington, and medical aid was summoned. It was found that be had received serious in- juries to the head and face, and he now lles in a serious condition.

HUTCHINSON-STREET PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. , WlDNES.—Services of thanksgiving for the harvest was I held in this place of worship on Sanday. Great taste had been displayed in the decoration of the building, a promi- nent feature being mottoes artistically executed by Messrs H Cooper and J Eardley. Both morning and evening the Rev Walter Graham preached eloquent sermons to good congregations, and in the afternoon the choir assisted by a few friends rendered the service of song " Harvest Echoes." Mr D Lewis conducted, and the harmonium was presided at by Mr (1 Parker. The narrative was read by Mr Samuel Draught. On Monday evening a well-attended fruit ban- quet was held under the presidency of Mr Thomas Rlllason. Addresses was delivered by the chairman and the Rev W Graham, Mr Drought, and Mr Shuttleworth. Fruit was served to the audience at intervals, and the proceedings were rendered additionally attractive by the singing of psalms and hymns by the choir. The collections and dona- tions amounted to upwards of £25. THE TALK OF THE Taws. Howell's Golden Herb Pills. Advt. THE LATE Ma. JoHN FlEavirr.—The body of this gentle- man, who who was deservedly respected in Runcorn and the surrounding distrtct, was interred in the cemetery on Wed- nesday. Mr. Hewitt, who had attained the age of 60 years, WBB a thorough Churchman, most earnest in his devotion, and it was his earnest desire to aid his fellowmen. His funeral, which was cenducted by Mr. Richard Morris, of High-street, Runcorn, was numerously attended, the greater Proportion of the tradesmen of the town attending as a last fitting mark of respect. The first portion of the service was conducted in St. Michael and All Angels Church, after which the mournful procession re-assembled, and a move was made for the cemetery, where the body was met by the Rev A Maitland Wood, M.A. who, assisted by one of his curates, read the remainder of the service in a most imp-es- sine manner. In the first mourning coach were Messrs El. 1 Thomas and Robert Hewitt .(brothers), Messrs George and ' William Hewitt (sons); and Mr John Weir. The bearers were the six nephews of the deceased, and the funeral was attended by members of the Runcorn Commissioners and tradesmen of the town. The service at the grave was full choral. From six to seven o'clock refreshments were pro- vided, and subsequently the Rev B Darhyshire, M.A., chaplain to Her Majesty's Forces at Altcar. took the chair. A ( OTTERY AT WIDNES.—On Monday at Widnes Police Court, William White, a tespectable-looking young man, of Liverpool, was charged with acting as a rogue and vaga- bond by keeping a lottery on the Market-ground, on Satur- day night. Police-constab)e,Norden said that he raw pri- soner on the Market-ground with a stand, on which he had displayed worthless rings, dm. He made a long speech as to the quality of the rings stating they ware "all gold ex- cept the inside, outside, and edges." He wrapped each ring in paper, and into some of the packlges he placed a three- penny piece; in consequence of that he sold about twenty- five at one penny each. Prisoner said be attended markets every day, and never was interfered with b-fore. He said he had a good character. Their w“rships were sitiefied be was carrying on a lottery, and fined him 103 and 12s costs, or in default one month.

ATTEMPED SUICIDE AT WIDNES —At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Elizabeth Bate, wife or Thomas Bate, North-street, Widnes, was charged with attempting to com• mit suicide by drowniag herself on Saterdey af!ernoon. George Laehlev, a workmen at Messrs Ornesiee'e, said that on Saturday afternoon he WAS working close to the iron bridee on the canal bank. Prisoner passed in the direction of Warrington. When about 150 yardeptst the bridge etie threw herself into the water. On seeing this, he along with another man named Edward Clarke, went and pulled her out. Police-constable Thompson said that from infor- mation he received be apprehended prisoner at her house in North-street, and charged her with attempting to commit suicide. She said In reply that she intended to do it, as her son had left her the previous day. She now denied to the magistrates that she threw herself into the canal, but said thaton walking alongthe bank she caught her foot and fell in. The husband ef the woman said he had never known her to doe thing like that before. She told him that she was fol. lowing her son who bat gone away. He would promise to take care of her. The magistrates discharged the woman with a caution. FATALLY CRUSHED by RAILWAY BUFFERS.—Mr Brig- house, county coroner, held an inquest on Wednesday on the body of John Barker, 23 years of • age, who lived in Edward-street, Sutton, who vas fatally erushed at Broad Oak Junction on Monday night. Mr Newton, from the locomotive department, Landon and Nortb-Western Rail- way, and Inspector Poole were present on behtlf of the railway company. James Fowl ea stated that he was an extra engimedriver, and deceased was an extra fireman. About twenty minutes past five o'clock on Monday after- noon they left the Sutton shed with three wagrops of coal and two of ashes to put there on a siding. Deceased got off •the engine to hold the points, and while witness was revere- log the engine the deceased uncoupled three of the waggons. Witness noticed them going into the siding, and said, "Jack, we shall have to leave Vaem all and take the engise hack." They were just moving, and deceased, of his own ' will, went underneath to uncouple the others from the en- gine. As coon as he had done so the waggons moved down the incline to the other three, which were then stetionary, and, rebounding, caught dveased between the buffers before be had time to get out. He was removed ta the Cottage Hospital and attended by Dr. Casey, but he died two hours later. Witness said there was no need for deceased to go ender while the waggons moved. They did not use slicks for uncoupling at the sheds —The Coroner add the case seelned a very simple one.—The Foreman rematked that deceased used his own discretion when to go between the waggons.—A verdict of " Accidental death " was re- turned. . -

- SHEEP-WORRYING. Sheep-worrying by dogs, which caused farmers between St. Helens and Wa”- rington considerable trouble and loss last winter, has again commenced. After the crops are gathered in many farmers agree with cattle dealers to find pasturage for cows, sheep, kc., at so much per head, and such arrangements are now being extensively made. On Saturday night Mr. Thomas Rylance, of Bold, left 74 sheep belonging to Mr. Fraser, of Knotty Ash, in the wood field on his farm. Early on Sunday morning lie went to see if they were safe, but found they had been scattered and worried by strange dogs. Seeing that one lay dead he went . back to the house, and Mrs Rylance and Joseph Rylance, his brother, continued the search. They found three sheep drowned in pits in different fields, the animals having rushed into the water to escape the fierce attacks of the dogs, and another was got out alive. Two more were injured, one having had its shoulder torn a w-ay. Six animals were missing, but were subsequently' found at Rainhill, two miles away. A watch was kept by two shepherds onSun- day night, but the worrying was n)t renewed. It is said that some persons in the vicinity keen their dogs fastened up during the day, but allow them liberty at night when they attack the sheep in the neighbourhood. FIRE AT ACTON GRANGE.—EarIy on Sunday evening a mounted messenger brought information to the Warrington Fire Brigade Station that a fire had broken out at the farm of Mr. Ball, Grange . Green, Acton Grange. The brigade, with the manual engine " Nile," proceeded to the scene, and their exertions were supplemented by the arrival of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co.'s fire engine "Victoria,' under the command of Mr. Thomas Ince, but the efforts of the combined forces had to be completely given to preventing the fire spreading. Twenty-one stacks of this season's produce were built within a score or two yards from the blazing mass of buildings. Considerable difficulty was experienced in. obtaining water, the supply being about 250 yards distant. The lire blazed all night, and it was not until Monday morning that the War- rington Fire Brigade could return. Even then Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company's engine was left to quench the smouldering ruins. The buildings are completely gutted, the whole of the damage amounting to about £l,OOO. The produce destroyed is valued at £5OO, and the buildings at £4OO. The owner of the property is Sir R. Brookes, Bart., and fortunately the whole is insured. The cause of the fire is supposed to be incendiarism. Much praise Ls due to the voluntary help of Messrs. Greenall's brigade, who heartily seconded the efforts 'of the Warrington men.

APPOINTMENT OF A HIGHWAY SUILVEYOIL—For the post of surveyor to the Daresbury Highway Board, vacant by the resignation of Mr. John Darby- shire, there have been 104 applicants. The success- ful applicant was Mr. llarold Peerman, of Chipping Sodbury, Gloucestershire. The applicants hailed from twenty-four different counties, and in ages ranged from 21 years to 58. The salary of the office is £l5O.

BICYCLING AT THE MANCHESTER EXHIBITION. —The finest bicycle racing ever seen in Manchester will be witnessed over the splendid track at the Exhibition on Saturday next, October 15th. On previous occasions only amateurs have been al- lowed to compete in the races promoted there, but this time the cream of the professional talent have decided to ride in a couple of rices, one of which is a ten miles professional scratch bicycle race for which the first prize is ..£l5. PENKETH WESLEYAN BIND Or MOPE.—Last evening week the committee of the Penketh Wes- leyan Band of Hope Society began their winter campaign, when they gave a most successful enter- , tainment in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. The chair was taken by Mr. W. Roberts, president of the Band of Hope Union, at 7-30 p.m., when an excellent programme was gone through. The recitations were well rendered, and were fully ap- preciated. Mr. Roberts gave a good practical ad- dress, which was well received. The society at Penketh is in a flourishing condition, having ex- cellent officers, of which Mrs. Garnett is president, and Mr. John Budden is secretary. There was a good attendance, and the meeting was very success- full.

DARESBURY llronwAv BoAnn.—A meeting of this Board was held in the Court Room, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Cliffe (vice-chairman) presided, and there was a small attendance ot mem- bers.—The Finance Committee reported that the balance in the treasurer's hands was £1,281 Is.—A letter was read from Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst calling the attention of the Board to the state of Heath- road bordering on the deep pool. It was, he said, very much sunk, and was in a dangerous and un- satisfactory condition, the wooden stumps of the railing round the pool were actually rotting for want of paint, and both the road and the railway adjoining the pool required immediate attention. This complaint had been forwarded to the Surveyor (Mr. John Darbyshire), who reported that he had been over the road twice and found that it was not sunk, that the wooden railings were net rotting for want of paint, and that the road did not want im- mediate attention. Those terms, he said, were ex- aggerations and misrepresentations, whoever had made use of them.—Mr. llazlehurst had been communicated with in regard to the report of the surveyor, and he replied that he had called at- tention to the matter, and he left further responsi- bility with the Board.—The matter then dropped.— The rest of the business was routine, and the Board ultimately adjourned till next Thursday, when the new surveyor (Mr. llarold Peerman) will enter upon his duties. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL CONTRACTOR AT RIINCORN.—On Wednesday, Mr. T. A. Walker, con- tractor for the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal, paid a visit to Runcorn. Mr. Walker was accompanied by Mr. fopham, and together the gentlemen walked through and surveyed the Old Quay yard, which is now the property of the Com- pany. Afterwards, tl-3 gentlemen proceeded along the shore to Weston* Point, and no doubt they would find much to interest them in the long line of docks through which they would have to pass. Having partaken of lunch, Mr. Walker and his com- panion went on board the steamer Ada, belonging to Mr. Ebenezer Timmins, engineer, Runcorn, and he was received by Mr. Charles and AIr.W. Timmins, sons of that gentleman. The vessel was at once put under weigh for Eastham, and on the voyage the visitors appeared to make a thorough inspec- tion of the proposed course of the canal along the Cheshire side of the river. Sub- sequently Mr. Walker and Mr. Topliam were put ashore' at Liverpool Landing Stage. In anticipa- tion of the great demand there will be for cottage property during the carrying out of the gigantic scheme a considerable quantity of land has been taken up during the past few weeks, and in one part of the town property is now in course of erec- tion. With regard to the river lrwell, it may be stated that it is very low between Barton and Irlam, and in consequence the Ship Canal Company's ! tugboats are engaged towing their vessels up the river at the latter place. It will be necessary to ob- tain a fresh supply of water for summer consump- tion, while the canal is in course of construction. , The line of canal from Barton via Irlarn and Cadis- head on to Warrington was, last week, inspected 'by Mr. Walker and his assisi,ants. Naxvies still continue to take up their residence in the Barton and Eccles districts.

div.head: GREBNWAY-ROAD SCHOOL -A MASTER TO BE APPOINTED.
div.p: GREBNWAY-ROAD SCHOOL -A MASTER TO BE APPOINTED.

The Clerk read the minutes of a special meetmg of the Board, held on Monday, September 26. Present—Mr. J. Pritchard (chairman), Dr. McDougall, E. Icnisrm, and F. A. Lake. Mr. E. M. Snevd Rynnersley, Her Majesty's In- spector of Schools, was also present at the invitation of the Board. —The Chairm in explained to Mr. Kynnerslev the circumstances under which his advice was sought with regard to the teaching staff of Greenway-road Board School.—An informal discussion followell, during which Mr. Kynnereley said he could not recommend the suggested appropriation of a class-room for infants, owing to the want of a separate playground and offices for them. He SAW no objection to boys being taught in the higher stan• dards, but in that case it would be necessary to revise the fees and obtain Departmental sanction to them. He thought It would be well to appoint a master as he had previously' advised the Board.—Mr. Lake, in order to being the matter to a vote proposed that a master be appointed to Green. aay-road School in place of Miss Hutchinson, and that the girls of No. 1 standard should be removed into the present girls' school, so that the school would practically cease to be a girls' school any longer. He would add to his resolu- tion that standards 1,2, and 3 be taught, and that a higher standard be added each year. He did not wish to encroach on other schools. They conld take their boys us. into the higher standards as they passed. whole question had Peen so well discussed that be thought he would say ,nothing further.--After a pause, Dr. Mc- Dougall seconded the resolution to open discussion, and re- served to himself the right of votinz against i- if he thought necessary.—tra reply to a question. the Clerk said there were on the rolls of the lower school 174 hove and 49 boys. The ettendance that (ley was 140 altegither, and there is accommodation for 274 scholars,—Mr Beckett said he ob. jected to Mr. Lake's proposition in toto. If the Board adopted the reeolution they would, he relieved, follow a mistaken policy. In the first place they would certainly have to encroach upon the domains o! the denominit'ocal schools in order to keep up a regular attendance at at-cc:a- way-road echools, and they were sure to do that, because of the differecce in the fees at that school, compared with the fees at other schools. Besides, the ratepayers would be pit to more axp-ms- by the additional stationery that would be required in the higt:er standards. Mr. Beckett argued from figures that he gave at the previous monthly meeting, the ex- pense of having a master at £l2O a year, Arc., would he ereater than keeping on the sgeool in its pr-er-nt form, with the additiam of an infant class which he argued was needed in the district where the FOIODI Woe situated. He concluded by moving thatthe school remain as it was, with additional accommodation for infants for the neighbourhood of Green- way-road.—The Clerk stated that there was at present school accommodation for 916 infants, and there were 856 infants on the rolls. The number in attendance was 597. Mr. Imison said he supported Mr. Like's proposition be- cause the figures quotA by the Clerk showed that there was no deficiency of accommodation for infants. There was, in fact, accommodation for 400 more than were in at- tendance. He should not like to encroach upon the denominational schools, and there was a safeguard because they proposed to limit themselves the first year to the third standard. He took exception to the figures laid before them by Mr„ Beckett.—Tbe Chairman supported Mr. Lake's proposition, on the ground that hitherto the echeol, as a mixed school. bad been a comparative failure. In the system p-opneed by Mr. Lake the B •ard would be amply repaid for any extra expense they might have to incur for a master.—Dr McDougall compli. He, however, thought the Board would be acting pruden ly, and in the interests of the schools, le taking the step proposed by Mr Lake. The gaestion of school fees would come up at a future date. As to the denotninational schools', the population of the town was not stationery; it cowinued to increase ; owl there- fore he dbi not far that th,re would be any entrenchment upon the denomina: ioeal schools. div.head: PROPOSED WEAVER TRUST INQUIRY.
div.p: THE PROPOSED WEAVER TRUST INQUIRY.

Upon the minutes of last meeting coming up for confirm- ation. Mr. Pritchard objected to the resolution agreeing to co-operate with the Runcorn Board of Guardians in ascer- taining the present position of the Weaver l'rust,with a view of securing that such Trust should be managed by trustees elected by the ratepayers of the county. Mr. Pritchard, whilst admitting that the amendment moved by himself was defeated, alleged that the proposition bad never afterwards been put to the meeting, although there were ten members present. The proposition, therefore, could not be carried.— The Secretary acknowledged that after the amendment was lost, the proposition was not put to the meeting. He, how- ever, made the minute perfect, as was his duty.—Mr. Pritchard Pointed out that the rules had not been complied with in the present instance, and the resolution was irregular and not binding upon the Board.—The Chairman said he had been a member of the Board for many years, and he had seen those rules enforced, but only on a few occasions.—Mr. Pritchard ought to have called the attention of the Boaid to the irregularity at the time (Hear, bear.)—After some further conversation, tho minutes were confirmel with the exception of the one in queation, and, wader the advice of the law clerk, the chairman moved,and Mr Taylor seconded, the suspension of the standing orders, so that the subject could be again considered.—Mr. Once then moved the reso- lution, and Mr. Taylor seconded.—Mr. Pritchard moved an amendment that tbe Board take no action in the matter ; and Mr. Grica said it was intended at present to merely I gather information, which would be placed before the county I ratepayers, and if they were satisfied with the management I of the Trust, nothing further could be done.—There was not I the slightest feeling against any member of the Weaver I Trust.—Mr Taylor remarked that the ratepayers had every- I thing to gain by the inquiry.—The Law Clerk said the Run- corn Guardians had agitated this matter for 15 years. It was owing to the action of the Guardians more than any- thing else that the Trust had made contribution to the county. By a published statement of accounts, the Weaver TruFt showed a revenue of £60,000, and out of that sum they bad paid £15.000 to the county. The Guardians thought there could be no harm to anysody if they could make impiries and 'fat the public know exactly how the Weaver Trustees stood with regard to the county ratepayers. —Upon being put to the meeting, the resolution was car- ried by six votes to four. The members who voted against were Messrs. Lake, Pritchard, ilanki uson, and Poison.
DR. McDOUGALL ON SEWER VENTILATION.

The Medical Officer presented the following report for September :—The number of deaths registered during the past month amount to 34. or these ens was an inquest case, and of the remaining 33 deaths, 8 were due to measles, 6 to consumptic n ot bswels, 2 to senile decay, 2 to typhoid fever, 3 to bronchial., 4 to disea.e of the grain, and one each to congesiion of the longs, inflammation of the liver, inflammation of the lining membrane of tbe brain, disease of glands, heart disease, chronic rheumatism, epilepsy, and chronic diarrhma. Exclusive tf the inquest case, the 33 deaths show an average death rate of 23 and a fraction per thousand of the estimated population, including the inquest case, of 21 per thousand.—By permission of the chairman, Dr. McD•ugall reported what seemed to him to be a highly dangerous method of sewer ventilation. This! ventilation consisted in allowing down water spouts to pass into sewers. He had oointed out in the case of property that had not been occupied more than seven or eight months, that al- though the spouts in front of the building had been eras- ted in accordance with knowledge and common sense, yet in the back parts of the buildings the down spouts des- cended one and all into the sewer. In one of these houses at the present time there was a case of typhoid fever, and within four inches of the bedroom window there was a loose joint in the water spout. He knew of no more ini• qnitous system of ventilation, and be cou'd not help ea. pressiog himself disappointed that, after whet he had brought before the Board on a former occasion, that property should have been allowed to he erected In the c inditton it was at the present time. He had endeavoured to ascerraln what source of fever existei in that particular house, and he cluld not find aay defect that would account for it. except the detect in the spout —The Law Clerk sug- gested whether it would not be best to deal with such a matter as this in committee —Dr. McDougall said it was information the Board ought ta receive ;he had nothing further to do with it. He sent A report with regard to theirs spouts before, and nothing was done. The committee would be asked to improve the defective drainage reported upon bY the inspector, benuse notices had been served UPON the owner.—Aftersome discussion as to what part of the doctor's remarks should not go before the public, the Chairman proposed that the Board go into comrnittee.—Mr.

ightburn s Aid the whole or none at all must he reported,— Mr. Taylor did not know that the Board had anything to hide. The doctor had !nide some rather serials charges. The inspector's rep,rr was new to him, and he was sur- prised th it it should he made to the doctor. and not to the Health Cominittee.—Dr. McDougall said the Health Com- mittee only mct once a month, and it would not do for thee, nuisances to exist for a month after they were slis- covered. The doctor then read the report, which referred to common brick traps in the back yards of the houses in ques- tion, which he condemned. Alla ling to the delths from measles, the doctor stated there was a want of care on the part of parents, and the children after measles then suffered from bronchitis. which accounted for these "deiths last month.—The Chairman said the myters brought forward were important, and, he hoped, would receive the attention of the committee concerned. He declined to allow any dfs• mission upon the subject, as it was not upon the agenda paper.—Mr. Lightburn and several other members expressed the opinion that these matters should come before the com- mittee ard then before the Board.

Car, emu --Mr. Mellor :This shows the folly of ru.hing through that appointment.—The Law Clerk ikto Mr. Timmins): If 'tat letter had been received you would have taken the ~cancy caused by Mr. Shaw's resignation.—Mr. Timm'aes said he must bid them all good-bye. lie had been con- nected with the Board for a quarter of a century, and know- ing other local authorities and town councils he could say that they were second to none in Runcorn.
