div.head: FELONIES AT WIDNES.
div.p: FELONIES AT WIDNES.

Messrs. H. Gaskell, jun , and Mr. J Brock were engaged a considerable time at Widnea Police Court on Monday, in- quiring into cases of felony. A middle-aged woman named Sarah Jane hicLaslin was charged with having on the sth September stolen a pair of bout% value 74 6d, the property of Patrick Horan, contractor, of 27, Lacy-street. The prisoner had been employed as a servant in Horan's house- hold. and when the boors could not 5e found she was ap- prehended br P.C. Holbrook, to whom she acknowlec4ed tier guilt. The woman alao pleaded guilty to having on the Mb July stolen a waistcoat, worth ss. belongiag to Peter O'Grady, labaurer, 28, Logsdale-read. The prisoner had been living at O'Grady's house, and it was sh)wn In evi- dence that she had pawned t'^e w..istcoat at the shop of James Carrot, Wuines-road, for 2s 31. She was sentenced to a month's imprisonment, a fortnight for cich offeLce„

Thomas O'Toole, a young man, was charged with stealing 14lbsi. of bacon, value Os, from toe shop of J. E. Johnson, provision dealer, Widnes road. About ten o'clock on Satur- day night John Wood, engine driver, in the employ of the Widnes Alkali Company, saw a man take a piece of bacon from a nail at the shop door, and walk along Gladstone. street. He informed the shop assistant, Aoel Parkinson, who gave pursuit and captured the thief. The prisoner had, however, rreviously thrown the bacon over a wooden fence. He was given into the custody of P.C. Holbrook, and as he was an old offender be was committed to the Quarter S?ssions for trial. Martin Mulvey. 17 years of age, who was described as dishonest by his father, was charged with ste.aling £ll in gold belonging to Edward Mulvay, labourer, 54, Wareing- street, his parent. On Sat ard iy morning Mulvey -placed eleven sovereigns in a box in his bedroom. The box was secured by a lock. At night the money had disappeared, and information was given to the police. Snspicion fell upon the prisoner, who was found at Ditton railway station at eleven o'clock os Skfhrlay morning by Win. Connor, of 27, Midwood-street. The prisoner, who was on his way to Liverpool, was brought back to Wida,s, and £8 7a 711 of the stolen money was found upon him. He was given into the custody of P.S. Robinson, to wham h 5 admiited li. guilt. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

Owen Tenser, a well-known character. was charged with stealing a basket contaioing 31b. of beef, a pound of bacon, and four eggs, the property of Owen Smith, of 22, Grove- street. On Saturday n;ght, about ten o'clock, Smith and his wife went into the vaults of the Stanley Arms to obtain some refreshment. Mm. Smith placed the basket on the floo. whilst she took out her curse to pay for the drinks she had ordered. Shortly afterwards she missed the basket. At this time William JO3eF, lodgiog-house keeper, Lugsdala- road. was watching a manhole in the road, and saw the prisoner, whom he knew very well, come from the Stanley Arms with a basket. Subsequently the prisoner offered to sell the basket and its contents to a man who, suspecting it was !realm threataned to kick him out of the house. Ulti- mately the prisoner succeeded in disposing of his spoil for Is to Patr ck Barks, of 10, Margaret-street. The value of the basket and goods was 58 63. When apprehended by P.S. McGregor, the prisoner said he knew nothing about the robbery. In reply to the newel questi ,ns the prisoner elec ed to ba dea't with by a jury, and the magistrates committed him to the Quarter Sessions.

div.head: WIDNES REVISION COURT.
div.p: WIDNES REVISION COURT.

The revision of the franchise list for the Widnes Division was resumed at Garman on ruesley by Mr .J T FOird, re- vising barrister, the Conservatives being represented by Mr W B Woodnorth, and the Liberals by Mr 11 B Shore. A WIDNES GEIsITLENIAN's CANDID CLAIM.—Mr Wood- north supported, on behalf of Mr John Walwvn Whhe, a claim for the lodger franchise in respect of the latter gentle- man's occupancy of two rooms at Lane-end-house, Hale- wood, and asked the Revising Barrister to amend the claim by inserting the words per annum " after Hee statement of value, which had been pat down at £l5 without any period being specified.—The Revising Barrister, however stated he could not do so. Although it could be done in a house- holders' claim, lodger claims stood in a different category. A person making a statutory declaration needed to be very precise in giving the nature of his claim for a I.:dger quali- fication.—Mr Shores remarked that Mr White resided with his father, a wealthy oil merchant.—The Revising Barrister said the fact of a father agreeing that his sons should have a vote was net sufficient to getalify the sons.—Mr White: But I actually do pay the money, and I can tell you candidly that my father has raised my salary so that I can pay the money to my mother. lion see lam very candid over it, sir.—The Revising Barrister : Yes, you are. But I cannot allow it —Mr White: you suggest how I can get a vote next year ? I think it is hard lines that I cannot get one. I want a vote badly.—The Revising Barrister said he wanted a bona ficle proof of rent and tenancy.— Mr White: This book is the only proof I can give; what more do yon require? The claimant added that his father did not usually vote for his residence, but for his qualification in Widnes.—The Revising Barrister said it was a case of steering between Scylla and Charybdis. but if Mr White claimed next year, and showed that his father did not vote in the township of Garston, be would seriously consider the matter. At present the claim was disallowed. On Wednesday evening Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barris- ter, commenced the revision of the list of Parliamentary voters for Widnes, Ditton, Cronton, Jec. The court was held in the police buildings. Mr. H. B. Shores was the Liberal representative, and Mr. W. B. Woodnorth officiated for the Conservatives. Mr. Guff, assistant overseer for Widnes, and Mr Houghton, assist ant overseer for Ditton, &c, were present to assist. NOT FOB THE SON-IN•LAW. James Bennett Jones claimed a vote as a lodger at the Beehive heerhouse, Albert- • road. Mr. Shores elicited that Junes was married and oc- cupied, with his wife and family, .two unfurnished rooms in the bowie for which he paid 43 per week.—ln reply to Mr. Woodnorth, Mr. Goff, the assistant overseer, stated that the rateable value of the house altogether was £2O a year —Mr. Woodnorth argued that this valuation was not sufficiently taro to allow two votes for the house, considering that there were 12 roocce is the building, and that there was a business in connection with it.—The Revising Barrister said that he had never allowed a vote before for a pay- ment of 4s per week, hut in this case he thought he should make en exception. He was Abiut to allow the claim when Mr. Woodnorth asked the applicant if he was any relation to the tenants of the house.—Son-in-law, re- plied Jones, and the Revising Barrister at once struck off the claim.

_ A POLICEMAN —James Brnce, a police constable, claimed a vote as the successive occupant of a house in ‘Valter- street knd No. 5, IVelmslev•atreet. There Was no objection, and his name was added to the list.

A CURIOUS CASE —James Eustace, a labourer, claimed a vote as the occupant of 15, Moon-street. The overseers objected.—Mr. G,iff said the property belonged to Mr. Jas. Muspratr, who had returned this particular house as empty. —ln reply to Mr. Shores. Eustace said he WSS Prepared to swear that he bad lived at the house for 15 years.--Nlr. Woodnorth demanded the production of the rent-book, but the applicant said he had not got one. The rent was stopped at the works.—The B mister : Mr. Muspratt does not return you amongst his workmen.---Enstace : I don't know anything about that.—The 'Barrister : You had better bring a note from the office allowing that you are employed there.—Eastace : I left there this fivo years. I work at Widnes Alkali now.—Mr. Woodnorth : You told us the rent was stopped at the works, and you worked there. Da you pay any rent ?—Enstace : Yes.—Mr. Woodnorth : Then where is your rent-book ?—Eastace : There is no rent-book.—The Barrister: Why have you not got a rent- book if you are a tenant of Mr. Musnrates, and do net work there.—Eustace: I don't know.—The Birrister : Yen must tell the truth before you are put on.—Bustace : 1 sin telling the truth.—Vote disallowed. THE NATIONAL LEAGUE OFFICES.—Mr. Shore-, on behalf Of M chiral Fcgarty, claimed a vote for the premises of the National League, St. Paul's Buildings. Fogarty slid the rent-bock was in his name, and Mr. Shores contended that the claimant was the only man the landlord could leualjv claim from. Fogarty, however, admitted that Dr. O'Keeffe paid the rent, and the claim was disallowed. Mr. J. T. Foard. revising barrister, resumed the revision of the list of voters for the township of Widnes, at the Local Bo rd Offices, on Thursday and Friday, and VariOßS Cases of the usual order were beard, and adjudicated upon.

Amongst the Mayor's communications were the following resolations passed at a public meeting held at the Co-opera- , tive Hall on Tuesdar, the 27th September, viz. :—L That , the Town Crunch l be requested to take immediate steps to make the Warrington Library free to all bnrgesses and in- habitants of the borough, as is already the case in the sur- rounding towns of Wigan, St. Helens, Runcorn, and Widnes, and in over 100 other towns in the United Kingdom.-2. That this meeting, having regard to the opinion of the Attorney-Cieneral, that "There is no authorit-, under the I Public Library Act of 1835 far making any distinction be- tween persons who subscribe and persons who do not," calls upon the Library and Museum Committee to cease to give special privileges to subscribers, and thus put all the rate- payers on a footing of equality before the law.-8. 1 hat the Town Clerk be requested to lay the foregoing resolutions before the Town Council at ite next meeting, and that the best thanks of this meeting be given to his worship the Mayor for calling the meeting, and for presiding.

ihe MAYOR : You will observe that there are three re- solutions submitted to the Council. We shall take the usual course and send them to the Museum and Library Committee for their consideration and then the matter will be discuss•cl at the neat Council meeting. .

Alderman CItaNDLEy : I quite agree —that that would be the best course to take with regard to the resolutions before us, but don't you think, sir, it would be advisable for the Council to have an opportunity of ventilating their opinions ou the subject? The Mayon : You cannot at this meeting. Alderman CHANDLEY My reason for suggesting so is that it might strengthen the hande of the Museum Com- mittee. if they heard an expression of feeling at this meet- ing. (Hear, hear). The MAYOR : Yes, but you cannot da it. Alderman CLIANDLEY : We cannot even discuss the sub- ject? The MAYOR : NO, it is irregular. Alderman Sorrow : lhe same thing occurred to me. I think, sir, you might have the power yourself to extend a privilege to the Council to exchange opinions on the subject as a preliminary to any further steps which may be taken. I think it would be of great assistance to the committee or to whoever have to go Into the question hereafter. If we ' could exchange opinions to-night —if you could grant per- mission to the Council—it would, perhaps, be labour that would not be altogether lost. (Hear, hear). The MAYOR : You see the resolutions have not yet been placed before the committee. Councillor W. PIERPOINT The committee have already discussed them. The MAYOR : I know that, but that is informal. Alderman Sorrow: I know it would not be in order to pass a resolution on the subject, but I thought -it possible yon might have the power to enable us to discuss the in it- ter, or to exchange opinions on the question, without coming to any riPcision on the subject. The Mayon : I arm only taking the regular course. Alderman SUTTON: Coilsidering that there is so much excitement in the town, it might be serviceable if we did go into it Alderman WEBSTER was understood to say that there was no great excitement in the town. Alderm in SuTrox : You have felt it, haven't you? Councillor H. ROBERTS: Can the standing orders not be suspended, Mr. Mayor. The MAYOR: No ; it is not a question of the standing orders.
Councillor ROBERTS : What will become of these reso- lutions ?
The MAYOR: They will be een t the Library Committee and then bruught before the Council. _
Councillor ROBERTS: With all respect, it seems to me a most absurd courso to Like.
Alderman SUTTON: It is no doubt the prrper course, but pPrhaps the Mayor would allow us to go into the matter.
Comelor HoLTotq: lias not something like thi3 already been before the Nlasoum Committee?
Councillor H. ROBERTS : Certainly. -

The MAYOR: I do not think we can go out of the regular course, and I would rather not. When it comes back from the committee the Council can please Nell what it does with the Committee's proceedings. As Alderman Sutton observes, it is rather an exciting question in the town, and that is one reason why the resolutions should be further considered. (Elear, bear.) I will call upon the Town Clerk to read a memorial. The matter then dropped. THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS —ALDERMAN BURGESS AND

div.head: MFL. DIGGLE.
div.p: MFL. DIGGLE.

The TOWN CLERK read the following memorial : " Memorial. To his worship the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington. We. the under- signed property owners and ratepayers of the Howley dis- trict, beg most respectfully to complain of the serious public nuisance arising out of and from the inercepting depot, and of the almost continuous passing and re-passing of the vans contiining the receptacles with excreta. Numerous complaints have been made previous to this to the Medical Officer and the Nuisance Inepector without in anywise abaing such nuisance. Your memorialists will ever pray," &c. There were, the Town Clerk added, between 50 signatures to this memorial. The MAYOR said he would take the usual course and for- ward the memorial to the Sahitary Committee for their consideration. The TOWN CLERK said there was also a memorial from the Ly thgoe's-lene district. He then read this memorial, which was similar in terms to the one already read, but had reference to Lythgoe's-lane depot. It was signed by from 60 to 100 persons.
The MAYOR said he would also take the usual course with regard to this memorial, and forward it to the Sani- tary Committee. Alderman BURGESS asked to _be permitted to say that if _ . .

those memorials were sent to the Sanitary Committee they would have ell the attention any committee could pay to a memorial. He would further say this much, that if a nuisance was preyed to exist through the instrumentality of the Sanitary Committee's depots, it could not be allowed to contieue. The Sanitary Committee could not be and never must be the creators of a nuisance offensive to the public. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR rennrked that that was not the proper time to discuss the matter.

Aldermin BannEss said he wasnot discussing anything; he was only telling them how they would deal with the matter. He wanted to ask permission to read a communication that had come to him. It had been sent by Mr. William Diggle. Might he be allowed to read it? The MAYOR If it is the wish of the Council. (Cries of " yes." Alderman BURGESS, resuming, said that Mr. Diggle wrote to him as follows—" Will you kindly oblige me, the undersigned, with an order to visit Longford depot to view the machinery and other plant, on Tuesday next, 4th inst." Mr. Diggle called upon him after having sent that Rote, and he (Alderman Bargees) told him very emphatically and very plainly and distinctly that he would not give him any such authority. (" Oh.") He bad good reasons for doing that. He received a good deal of insolent abuse from Mr. Diggle for it, but that was a matter of very little moment, only they might be protected from that sort of thing. Mr. Diggle told bin that be would see the Mayor, and be told Mr. Diegle that he might ipe the Mayor, but that the Mayor could not give him an order.

The MAYOR: He has not seen me. Alderman BURGESS continued that Mr. Diggle said he would go without anthority, and that day when he west to Longford with a deputation immediately he got on the pre- mises he saw Mr. Diggle himself there, without any author- ity from anybody ; and it appeared that previous to that he had got inside the premises and was as the platform ex- amining the m tchinery before anybody knew he was there, but he was removed. And inasmuch as there was a resolu- tion of that Council authorising that he (Alderman Burgess) alone should give authority to visit the works he meant, so far as he was concerned, to carry out the in- structions ef that Connell, and he wished to say for the information of the Council that if any member of the Council took with him any other person that other person would be refused permission. There was a member of the Council who asserted that he had done that, but in that case he (Alderman Burgess) thought it was a very im- proper use of the power given to the members of the Council.
The matter then dropped. WATCH COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee it wasr.resolve that Police. constable Jones be promoted to the first class, with the in- crease of a shilling a week. On the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor JOLLEY, the minutes of this committee were adopted. El/UWE COMMITTEE.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. This cos mites kad resolved that the tender of the Coal- brookdale Company, Limited, to supply a breeze tablet to mark the site of the ancient Austin Friary at 140 s be ac- cepted. The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes.—Alder- man HOLMES seconded the resUution, mad it was passed. THE LONGFORD MANURE WORKS AND THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. COMICIIIOr BARKER moved :—" That the Sanitary Com- mittee be requested to give to the Council, at its meeting in November, a fall, true, And detailed account of the working of the machinery at Longford and the intercepting depots, showing at the same time the quantity of excreta and refuse sent to the intercepting depots and to Longford, the quan- tity of concentrated manure manefectured, and the cost Der ton of making the same." In doing so, Councillor Barker said that the question was a repetition of what he asked some time ago, and he WAS then requested to wait until the committee had had an opportunity of thoroughly testing the machinery at Longford depot. He was not going Into the questioe of the depot that night, as all that be required was that the Council should ask the Sanitary Committee to give the information in November next. Councillor W. PIERPOINT seconded the motion, remark- that the toe-meet was a reasonable one, and that he hoped the chairman of the Committee would place no obstacle in the way. Alderman BURGESS: Certainly not. The resolution was then passed. A onusTro. Ceuncillor MACEIR said he thought that was the proper time to put a question concerning the fact that three resolu- tions that he had sent a fortnight before the last Town Council meeting had never been entered on the notice paper although they referred, he thought, to some of the most im- portant matters that concerned the town. A year ago some papers were lost in their progress from ratepayers to the Council, and he should feel sorry to think that the same thing should be happening now. He was precluded, he pre- sumed, from referring to the matters from the fact that his , notice had notaopeared. It was not for the want of any careen hie pert, because he eupp'ierl them twice over. To-' matter was of the greatest importance to the ratepayers of Warrington, and the Town Council as tha manufacturers of gas, proprietors of water, aod dealers in sewage, and those subjects were dealt with in a short,and as be thought, pithy manner. He should be glad to know how be could now get the thirg before the Council Cr the public. The MAYOR said that he would confer with the Town Clerk on the subject, and see if the matter cmld be brought forward. The Towx CLERK: The notices were of such a nature that it was imposeible to put them on the minutes. This was all the business.

div.head: SANITARY COMMITTEE.- THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS AGAIN.
div.p: SANITARY COMMITTEE.- THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS AGAIN.

At a meeting of the Sanitary Committee, held on the 7th September, it was resolved that Miss Walker he appointed matron of the Hospital for Infectious Diseases at a salary of $4O pernonnth. It was also agreed that the report of the Medical Officer of Health for 1886 be approved and sub- mitted to the council. The report was submitted to the Council some time ago,but was not adopted, as it was con- Ridered necessary to make an alteration in it. An alteration was made in the paragraphs beaded "The Chief Sanitary Requirements of the Borough," which now read as follows: —"I desire to draw your attention 10 my report of 1885 re- lative to unsanitary dwellings and unpaved streets and back passages. I have so often referred to the danger to health arising from the open spaces around houses being en- croached on by the buildieg of pigeon cotes, fo vi pens, Aze., that I have only to remind you that little or no improve- ment has been made during the year. In conclusion, there is one other occasion of nuisance which I feel it my duty to name to the Committee, inasmuch as it might be the origin of infectious disease, and must therefore be dealt with by the Health Committee—l refer to the sewers. This has been under notice in previous reports, and I mention it now In order to express my satisfaction in hawing received an assurance from the Paving and Sewerage Committee that they feel their respoestibility in this 'matter, and that they have taken active steps in a case I brought to their notice. This renders it unnecessary for me to make any detailed statement in the present report."—At a meeting of the Com- mittee held on the 14th September it was resolved that the tender of Mr. John Buckley, for suppl ying horse hire for the next three months a, 63 101 per man and horse per day, be accepted, and that upon the recommendation of the Privy Council the following regulations beimade and put in force: —"Borough of Warringtnn. The Contagious Haw:aerie (Animals) Acts, 1878 to 1886. The Animals Order of 1886 Swine fever. Notice is hereby given, that at a meeting of the Local Authority of the boroaigh of Warrington, held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday, the 14th day of September, 1887, the said local authority, for the purpose of preventing the spreading of swine fever, made the regulations following that is to say :—These regulations shall commence and take effect from and immediately after the let day of Oct deer next, and shall continue in force until the 20th day of No- vember next, unless sooner reaoked or altered by the Local Authority of the borough of Warrington. No market, fair, auction, or exhibition of swine shall be held within the bor- ough. Dated this 27th day of September, 1887. W. HENRY BROOK. Town Clerk." Alderman BURGESS moved the adoption of the minutes. Alderman SUTTON seconded. Councillor PLATT said he was glad to hear from Alderman Burgess that if a nuisance was proved to exist the Sanitary Committee would take step: to put an end to it. He did not know what proof Alderman Burgess wanted, but if serious, continuous complaints since the intercepting depots were established were any proof, then the Sani- tary Committee had proof enough. He coald say himself that the Lythgoe's-lane depot was a most harmful and hrirtful nuisance, because he spent about twelve hours a day in the neighbourhood. It had a most . . _

serious effect on his own hearth arid upon the health of everybody living in the neighbourhood. Perhaps Alderman Burgess would tell them n hat proof would be suf- ficient, and they would go the right way about providing it. These depots were a standing dis- grace to the Corporation and to the Sani,ary Com- tnittee. It was almost incredible that in these days of sanitary enlightenment the Sanitary Committee should have put down plant of that description in the most densely populated neighbourhood. Any person of ordinary com- mon sine might have known that material of the sort •

taken to the deiamts could not he manipulated in the way it was done without creating a nuisance. For bis part he said it was a decided ruisance and a very serious one. He had himself written four or dve times to tbe fianit try Commit- tee, but never yet had a reply. In his laat letter he asked distinctly for a reply, and be got one to the effect that the chairman of the committee was away from home, but that he should hear from him when he returned. Since then two meetinns had been held, but be bad beard nothinz fur..
ther. He thonullt it WAS. Scarcely courteous treatrne-nt for

any ratepayer—he claimed no exceptional privilege—to be met with time after time when he made a serious complaint of that kind. (lieu, hear.) It was high time the Sanitary Committee took the matter in hand, not with the determi- nation to stick to what they had done through thick and thin, bu, to look into the matter and judge from the effect it bad upon the health of the people living in the neigh- bourhood. No one could suppose that 9Och depots would have been allowed to be put down, say in Palmyra-rouare— (hear, bear,)—and he said that thp ratepayers in the neigh- bourhood of these depots had as much right to live in peace land comfort, and with as much pure air as possible, as those in any other part of the town. But they did not get this pure air. They were poisoned, aye, poisoned de- liberately, because their health was endangered by the emanations of those depots. He did hope the chairman of the Sanitary Committee would take that matter in hand from an independent point of view. (Hear, bear.) Councillor BOLTON referring to the Medical Officer's re- port said that complaints were made in it as to Meters. War- ing'e tannery. It seemed rather peculiar that the officials of the Sanitary Committee could smell that, because if they went to the ieterceotine depots they could smell something more offensive than the most offensive trade. It did seem something of an anomaly to talk about offensive trades, and then go on to speak about the successful working of the intercepting depots. Conncillor Dixote said there wan a statement in the medi- cal officer's report which was not correct. It stated that the machinery at Longford had been brought to perfection in the manufacture of manure, but it had taken five years to do that, while other people bad been at it right away from the year 1881. Councillor H. ROBRRTS : The report does not state that. Councillor DixoNr : Then I must have read it wrong. Councillor ROBNRTS : You have. (Laughter). Alderman SLITTON :That is nothing to do with yombut you are a member of the School Attendance Committee. (Laugh- ter). _ . _
anttneillor DIXON : I am, but I am not a member of this intelligent committee. and the report we got from Alderman Sutton respecting the breakdown of the machinery was not _
such an .intellrgent one. !Laughter.) The intercepting depots were anything but what was said in the medical officer's report, and they did not need to go far for proof of that.

Alderman BURGESS, in replying, said he had nothing to state in reference to what had passed beyond what he stated at the outset. If they thought that the intercepting depots were a Nuisance that nuisance must and should be abated, whatever the cost. Not a word was said about the Longford depot. With the exception of Councillor Dixon, nobody was ready to take up the cudgels against it ; bet so long as they had the support of that Council in carrying out work which they have delegated to them, they would try to do it to the satisfaction of the Council, and to the satis- faction of the public at large. If they expected more from them—if they expected them to do something more for in- dividuals than they did for the whole community— they would not attempt it ; but this they would undertake —that any work which they had in hand should be con- ' ducted in such a way that no reasonable person could com- plain. (Hear: hear). . .
The resolution we then put and agreed to. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMW/TTEE.

This committee, at a meeting held on the sth September, resolved that the footpath in Wilderspool Causeway be con- tinued to the end of Mornington-terrace, and that the tender of the Warrington elate Co., Limited. for the supply of 300 tons of four inch granite sets at 20s (id per ton, delivered by boat at Whitecross Wharf, be accepted. div.p: RUGBY RULES.

WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. DITTON.—ThiS match was Played on the ground of the former, and after a pleasant game resulted in a win for the home team by three tries and eight minor, to two minors. Wvcherly scored twice and Rowlinson once for the home team. ' FRODSHAM 2ND V. WIDNES TREE BLUES 2wn.—Plaved at Frodsbam, this being the first match the second team have played. The Frodsham players might have played with more judgment, hut after a pleasant game the match ended in a drew—Frodsham, 1 try (Caldwell) 2 miners ; Trun 81ue,,, 1 try 5 minors.

FARNWORTIE V. INCH CONSERVATIVES FIRST TEAM.— These teams met at Ince on Stturday,, and after a pleasant and well-contested game the match resulted in a draw in favour of Parnwrtli by five minors to three minors. Farn- worth would have scored several times but for the fine play of the lace caPtain, who played a splendid full back game. All the Farnworth team played a good game. _ _

WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL V. WYCLIPEB let TEAM. —This match was played on Saturday. Fisher kicked off for the school, and play was at once taken into the Wycliffe 25, two minors being quickly scored, followed shortly after- wards by a try, which Fisher converted into a splendid goal Wycliffe however then showed up scoring a try and a minor in quick succession. On chanee of ends, the Wycliffe for- wards had much the best of it, the whole time however con- sisting of one long series of scrimmages, the chief features being the fine forward play of several of the Wycliffe team led by Bate and Picton, and the fine saving of Haynes for the school. The game ended in 1 goal 4 minors for the Grammar School and 1 try 7 Inie,,re rot Wycliffe. Team, Grammar School :.Full back, Webster; three.qsarter backs, Fisher, Littlewood, Bru.drett; half backs, Haynes and Kneriman ; forwards, Kidd, T Williamson, W Williamson, R Williamson, Hannah, Whittle, McFall, Linaker, Horton. Wycliffe: full back, Knowles; three-quarter backs, Hamer,. Brown, W Lowe; half bias. it Ball, 0 Barker; forwards Bate, Booth, It Lowe, Summers, Cotton, Yonge, Picton• Taylor, Hayes. FBODSTIAI/ v. ST. CLROPAS LIVERPOOL.— Frodsham journeyed to Liverpool, on Saturday, in pleasant weather, and after an arrangement of two half hours the Saints kicked off. A good return being made brought about a scrimmage in centre, and after a spirited run by Rogers and kick into touch, J. Dimelow got the ball and crossed the line in an easy manner, the kick at goal being a poster. From the kick out Frodsham again worked the ball over. which resalted in a minor. This brought half-time. Dar. lington re-started for Frodsham. No return being made, a scrimmage wee formed in the Saints' 25, but the Saints drew away and worked the ball into the visitors' 25. Webb here broke away, but was brought down in the Saints' 2:5, and after a severe scrimmage the Saints got the ball in neutral ground. Here no aide was called, which left Frodsham vic- tors by one try four minors to one minor. Frodsham backs all played well ; their passing was rather interrupted by the Saints' halves playing off-side, repeatedly collating the Frodsham halves before the ball came out of the scrimmage. The forwards all played well, Molynena being the most conspicuous of the pack.

WIDNES V. ST. frELENS.—These teams had their first en- counter for the season at Widnes, on Saturday, when the home, team, notwithstanding that three of their backs, Par- kinson, Plumpton, and Farrell, were absent, and that their opponents had their strongest team on the field, won a well- contested game by one goal, one try, and fire minors, against three minors. At the opening the home team played up finely, and before the game was many minutes old, Norris, by a splendid flying kick, sent the ball over the cross bar. After that Widnes pressed hard, and scored four minors in the first half, Howard and Morris making futile attempts to drop a goal, and Wilkinson making the best run of the game, taking the ball from the centre to his opponents' line, where he was knocked into touch. After the change of ends St. Helens played with great dash for a white, scoring three minors, and narrowly missing a goal from a fine drop by Haselden, the ball hitting the uprights. Just be- fore the cell of no side, when Widnes were pressing hard, Smith ran in from the quarter and secured a try near the 25 fia4, which Morris failed to improve. The Widnes for- wards were by far the superior lot, but the hacks were more evenly matched. These teeing met at Runcorn on Saturday. Having de- feated Rochdale Hornets the previous week when they first donned the jerseys for the season, the home team were con- fident of achieving a similar pleasing result with Salford, and upwards of 3,C00 persons assembled to witness the en- counter. It was decPed to play ,35 minutes each way, and Hughes, winning the tow, Ottiwell kicked off for Salford. 'Phrough a" mull "a scrimmage took place in Runcorn 25. A line out shortly afterwards teok place, and Kent got over the line. Anderton's kick at goal was a failure. At last a beautiful chance occurred. Andrews neatly got hold from a scrim- mage, and passed to Speakman,whie would have had a short straight run in under the posts, but the champion three- quarter was a little off colour, fumbled the ball, and the chance was gone. BARROW. -This match was played at Warrington on Saturday, nearly 4.000 spectatori being present. The visitors arrived early in the morning,' and it was apparent that they had not mus- tered their full strength, as Forshaw,. Harley, Woedburn, Kitinish, and Lake were absentees. The home team was the same as advertised, with the exception of R. Littlewood, Donohue being the substitute. Two thirties having been agreed en, Gregory, as captain of the visitors, started the oval, and no return being made the first scrimmage was formed in Warrington territory. Warren was the first to make any movement by a short run to half-way, bat was well tackled by Mawson. From the scrimmage Speakman gave Jolley a chance, but be was too well watched by Gre- gory who was next conspicuous by a goed run from his own quarter flag to the home team's twenty-five, being brought down by Buxton in grand style. By passing the Barrow backs gained a little ground, and Lewis was collared with the ball in his possession. The " wirepullers," not to be denied,.took the leather back to the visitors' territory, the rash being nicely saved by Gregory. From a scrimmage formed on the line a deceptive pass by Warren enabled him to gain a meritorious try, Speakman kicking a neat goal Furgusson re-started from the centre, play for a short time settling down in mid-field. A neat dribble and good kick by Frank Turner again removed operations to the visitors' lines. A free kick was here awarded Barrow, but nothing was gained. Passing by Fair Turner, Warren, Barnes, and Massey almost ended in the latter scoring, but he was pushed into touch on the line. The Barrow forwards gradually worked the ball back to centre field. The home team pressed the visitors hard, but Marsh replied with a timely kick to quarter fine. The Warrington forwards again broke away, and took the ball over the line, the ball rolling into touch-in-goal. Furgusson dropped out, Warren returning with interest. Splendid exchange kick• lug was next witnessed between Marsh and Barnes, the play finally settling close to tee visitorea lines. A scrim- mage was formed, and Warren passed to Barnes and that player to Jieley, who made a short run, but being pressed dropped a splendid goal amidst deafening cheers. The game being restarted, some pretty passing ley Barnes, Speakman. and Massey took play to the Barrow 25. A good kick by Fair. Turner removed the ball into the visitors' lines, where from a scrimmage Warren passed to Barnes, who transferred to Massey, the latter getting over. The point was, however, disallowed on the plea of "thrown forward." The visitors removed operations to centre-field, and when half-time Was called the score stood—Warrington two goals, 1 minor ; Barrow nil. The game was recommenced by Frank Turner, the ball going in touch at the quarter flag. Baucher and Alexander broke away with the ball at their toes, but this movement was checked by Bar'nes, and play finally settled at centre. Neat passing by Fair. Turner and Massey ended in the latter punting to the Barrow lines, the ball being well returned by Marsh. A rush by the Barrow men was stopped by Barnes kicking to mid-field. The visitors now became dangerous, and Massey saved by kicking dead. Frank Tur- ner dropped out. Give and take play followed, until Lewis and Leaks relieved the monotony by passing to the home team's quarter flag. MaWson was here awarded a free kick, but nothing came of it. Lewis next "made his mark." but Buxton relieved by a good kick to half-way. From the line out some passing by the home team forwards took the leather in dangerous proximity to the visitors' goal, but the Berrew men relieved to nalf.way, and, from a scrimmage formed here, Warren passed to Jolley, who got clear of all opposition except Marsh, the latter player bringing him down in grand style. The home forwards took the ball over the line, Rancher saving by kicking dead. The came player restarted, Massey returning well in touch. Marsh relieved his lines by a good kick to Buxton, but that player Wee too safe to allow the visitors any opportunities, and he transferred the oval back again. From the pack Speakman passed to Massey, the last-named making a grand

NOTES BY 'FR PI WAY. The contest on Saturday between Warrington and Barrow was, owing to its rather otee-sided character,not of the high. eat interest. It gave further evidence, however, that War- rington are this season going thoroughly in for intelligent high class play, for it W4i llCldollbtedly in the fine unsellih passing that they excelled their opponents more than in anything elee. Barrow turns out a stalwart lot of forwards arid when it came to a set scrimmage it took the benne team all their time to hold their own,but when open play was the, order of the day, they were sadly deficient. It is combine- tion "as does it" and Warriagton had the combination. Warren's try was thoroughly deserved and was a very popular event with the spectators. This halt-back has pao• isably done more than any other individual player to gain 1 the initial victories for Warrington. At the same time ' and even if he keeps up the same form throughout it would not be surprising if at the end of the season he is some elle- tonne from the top of the 114 with rezard to points to his Credit. Ile displays the greatest merit of a half back.unsel- fishness, and he does not seek to shine on his awn account when parting with the ball is likely to help,llll side. . War- riczton is strong in its threrknuatters,and so far Warren has sought to give them plenty to do. Walton were badly mauled on their own ground, on Sat- urday, by Warrington "A" team. Whittle's contingent allowed up splendidly in the passing game, and simply walked round their opponents. It is to be hoped the Wal- tonians will take to heart the rather severe lesson they have received, and copy the superior tactics of the Warrington. lane. We may than find when they come to play their re- turn match in January that adversity has had Its uses in their case.

HARVEST FESTIVALS. ST. PETER'S MISSION, WARRINGTON. On Sunday a harvest thanksgiving service was held at St. Peter's Mission. The Mission was very neatly decorated in the customary fashion. The sermon at both the morning and evening service was preached by the Vicar (the Rev. G. D. Wray). At the evening service an anthem, "0 Lord, how mani- fold are Thy works," was well rendered by the choir. The collections were on behalf of the day school, and amounted to .E 1 13s Bd. The decorations were carried out by Miss Jones, Miss Holley, Mies Sykes, Miss Mary Annie Sykes, Miss Frances Sykes, Mr. Joseph Sykes, Miss Ada Culm, Miss Lizzie Heaton, Miss Edgar, Miss Jane Edgar, Miss Pugh, Miss Crompton, and the Misses Rachel Crompton, Annie Balshaw, Victoria Balshaw, Alice Warburton, Polly Perry, Mrs. Smith, Mr. S. Welling, and Mr. R. Welling.

div.head: ACADEMY-STREET MISSION. _ .
div.p: ACADEMY-STREET MISSION. _ .

_ At this Mission on Sunday and Monday services were held to celebrate the season's ingathering. The room was prettily decorated, the work having been done by the ladies connected with the mission. On Sunday sermons were preached by Mr. Evans; and on Monday evening a tea and fruit banquet were held, about 100 persons sitting down to the former. Mr. W. Hickman presided at the after meeting, when singing and recitations were gone through, interspersed with abort addresses by Messrs. J. Taylor, Power, Roscoe, Cook, Parker (Stretton), and Miller. A vote of thanks was heartily passed to the chairman for his services. No collections were made at the Sunday services, there being only the ordinary offertory box. The proceeds, were over £6.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

On Sunday, harvest thanksgiving services, inclu- ding two celebrations' of the Holy Communion, were held in Orford Church, and were well attended all day, the evening congregation completely filling the building. The Rev. I Phillips chaplain of Or- ford, preachettin the morning, and gave a catache- tical address in the afternoon at the children's ser- vice. The e,vening preacher was the Rev. Joseph Pulliblatik, Senior Diocesan Inspector of Schools; 'who gave an able sermon from the text' They joy before thee according to the joy in harvest." The services were hearty and the singing well ren- dered, especially the anthem "All thy works" (Pat- ,tison), which was very creditable to the members of the choir and singing class. The church was beautifully decorated, handsome and appropriate texts, devices, &c., adorned the walls, chancel screen, and other parts of the edifice.. A cleverly- executed model of a stack-yard, the work of , Mr. James Swinton, of Orford, was much and deservedly admired, and reflected great credit on the intelli- gent pains that had evidently been bestowed, the words "All is safely gathered in" worked in grain on the roof of the well-stocked Dutch barn being particularly appropriae. The decorators included Mrs Beamont, Mesdames Phillips, Mortimer, C. Grounds, and J. Swinton, the Misses Shaw Hill, Howard, Hooper, Woolmer, and Clare;- and Messrs Cann, C. Grounds, W. Turner, and Zeal. Grain, fruit, vegetables, and flowers were contributed by several members of the'congregation. The offerings, which amounted to .£lO 17s sd, were given to the Diocesan Institutions. , LYMM. PARISH CHURCH. . _

The harvest festival in connee—tien. with St. Mary's, Lymm, was held on Sunday. There was an early celebration of Holy Communion at 8 a.m., the Rector and the Rev. E. W. Lomax officiating. The morning prayers were intoned by the Rev. G. W. Guest, the lessons being read by Mr. Walter Heslop, M.A., of the Grammar School. The sermon was preached by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington, who took for the subject of his discourse "The harvest is come "—St. Mark iv. 29. In the afternoon these was a procession of Sunday school scholars from the schools to the church, the various banners belonging to the schools being car- ried in procession. At 3-30 a children's service was held in the church, when an address on "Angels" was given to the children by the Rector. The even- ing service was preached by the Rev. IP:Wainwright vicar of St. John's, Altrincham, who took his text from 1 Cor. xv. 51, "Behold, I show you a mystery." The decorations this year were again of a very com- plete and high-class character. Amongst those engaged in the work of decoration were Mrs. Guest, Mr. Gibbes, Mrs. Lomax, Misses Bayley, Major and Mr. E. P. Browne, Miss Battersby, Mrs. Dearden, Mrs. Hardwicke, Mrs. Ardern, Misses B. Evans, E. Gregson, Morris, and Morton, Mrs. Adden- brooke. Misses Pothecary, theXisses Stubbs, Misses Brabazon, and Mrs. T. P. Norris. The congregations throughout the day were very large, and the collec- tions, which are to go- towards defraying the cost of enlarging and re-arranging the organ, amounted to slightly over £lB.

Mr. Bright, in a letter to Mr. Arthur Elliot, M.P., strongly condemns the establishment of A Parliament in Dublin. Mr. Bright hopes that Liberals will not knowingly make a cur- render which may be fatal, humiliating, and ignominious. THE CHUROH CONGRESS —The Church Congress, which , opened with the Presidential address from the Bishop of Lich- , field on Tuesday. promises to lee a great success, nearly 2,300 tickets having been sold. The subjects chosen for discussion are varied, and it is expected will give rise to very interesting debates. The Mayor gave a reception on Monday afternoon aster the arrival of the Archbishop of Canterbury, who, in response to the welcome, said he was glad they were inviting working men, not only to listen but to join in their discussions, because he believed in future they would take a great part in supporting the Church and Christianising the country. The Congress was opened at Wolverhampton in the Drill Hall, nearly 2,000 persons, in- cluding the Archbishop of Canterbury, being present. The presidential address was delivered by the Bishop of Lch- field. His lordship reviewed at some length the history of the Church of England during the last twenty years. Th y accepted, as Churchmen, the supremacy of the Crown: but the supremacy of Parliament was another matter; and tit( y might need to be delivered from it as from a Pope. Tee Archbishop of Canterbury followed. The work of the Con- gress then commenced, a discussion taking place on the sub- ject of the Church and history. In the afternoon the Bis- hop of Lichfield again preached, and there was a very large attendance. At the Church Congress,ion Wednesday morn. log, the subject of discussion was the rapid growth and movements of the population, the particular points dealt With being migration, emigration and colonization. Mr. Rankin, spoke in favour Of the formation of village emigration clubs for facilitating the saving el money by ' intending emigrants.

WHY DID THEY SMILE.—" Yes, my hands are soft," said a conceited young fellow the other night in a small company, as he admiringly looked at those useless ap- pendages that had never done a day's work. "Do you know how Ido it?" he exclaimed proudly. "I wear gloves on my hands every night to sleep in." "Do you sleep with your hat on also ?" asked a pert young woman. And the young fellow replied in the negative, and looked wonderingly because the company smiled. "A WOMAN'S PROMISE."—Mr. Daniel S. Dickinson, formerly United States senator from New York, who was very fond of saying sharp things, sometimes gave offence by his witticisms when he least expected to do so. One day, when he was walking moodily along the street in Albany at the time Silas Wright was governor, he met Mrs. Wright, the governor's wife. Observing his abstracted air, she said, in a jocular manner, " What does a man think of when he is thinking of nothing?" , "Of a woman's promise," responded Mr. Dickinson. "Well done, senator," said Mrs. Wright, who passed on, but did not forget Mr. Dickinson's remark. Some time , afterwards he requested her to help him to persuade the ] governor to appoint a friend to office, reminding her at 1 the same time that she had promised to aid him when- ever he should ask for her assistance. "That is true, senator," she replied; "but of course it was nothing." "How is that ?" exclaimed Dickinson, much surprised. "Because it was a woman's promise, don't you know ?" responded Mrs. Wright. The senator did know, and he had to tell his friend that the "adverse influences " were so strong that the coveted appointment could not be obtained for him. A CURIOUS COINCIDENCE.—He was an exile, poor fellow, and glad to meet a man who knew of the parts from whence he hailed. "Yes, sir," he said, "I lived in New York myself for four years." And then you went ] to Milwaukee ?" "Yes, sir; that's where I landed next." " Strange to say it was that city I struck myself after leaving New York. Fine town, Milwaukee." " Yes; I was quite sorry to leave there, but business ere long called me to—" "Denver." "Yes, sir, you're i right, Denver. Now there's a booming city—regular stem-winder. Ever been to Denver ?" " Yes, siree. Denver is a pretty slick sort of a place. Didn't stay there long, eh ?" "Just a few days, but long enough to become quite in love with the city. I went to Kansas after leaving there." "Kansas ?' (referring to his note book). " Yes, that's right, you were just twelve hours ahead of me there." "Well, seems to me, stranger, we have travelled much over the same ground. Curious coincidence, ain't it ?" "Ye-es, 'tis a trifle funny, mate, but the best of the joke has to follow. We now go to New York. After all New York is the only place worth ] living in. Any objections to exchange cards? There's mine." It reads—" Jack Phipps, Detective, New York." "This is my warrant for your arrest. Embezzlement; that's it. Curious coincidence, ain't it ?"

capable of expressive modulation ; and, (6) in emotional pieces, to have their pasions portable, bottled-up and entirely under control. After the piece is concluded, bow and walk off. Do not grasp eagerly at any and every excuse for taking "a call ;" your own self-respect should guide you in this. If the audience continue to applaud BO heartily as to justify an encore, let it be short, and of a bright and humorous character, and thereby give them no reason to curse the rashness which prompted the applause. Tbe recitor who would succeed in satisfying an in. telligent audience must go through a course of care- ful training, and to this end we would commend a work on" Elocution" published, as is the case with tit The Thespian Papers," by Mr. Walter Scott. This new work is the joint production of Mr. T. R. W. Pearson, MA., of St. Catherine's College,Cambridge, and Mr. F. W. Waithman, lecturer on elocution in the Leeds and Bradford Institutes. "This little primer" it is stated in the introduction," is in nowise designed to supersede the many exc.:ollmA treatises on elocution now in use ; its main object is to place within the reach of all the means of mastering the simple princi- ples of an art becoming daily more and more requis- ite and popular, and to supply a useful and portable class book hitherto unattainable." The work deals in the first place with the voice, breathing, and articu. lation, and then proceeds to " pause and inflection," and "gesticulation," while there is a general chapter on common defects in readers and reciters. The volume concludes with a number of selected recita- -1 tions in prose and verse. "The Turkish Bath," a sixpenny pamphlet of 100 pages, will be welcomed by all who make use of that invaluable institution. It is written by Mr. F. C. Co- ley, 11. D., and its scientific statements may therefore be depended upon. Some idea of the range of the book may be gathered from the contents, which are as follows :—History of the Turkish Bath, How to take a Turkish Batb, Rules for the Turkish Bath, The theory of the Turkish Bath, on Errors, and Appendix. The chapter on the theory of the Turkish Bath makes plain much that many less learned writers have pre- sented in a confused and unsatisfactory manner. Al- together this pamphlet is by far the best work on the subject we have seen. Another sixpenny pamphlet which we have received from Mr. Walter Scott is entitled "Parental Com- mandments." It is a series of "Warnings to Parents on the Physical, Intellectual, and Moral Training of Their Children." The following page of t' Dents" is a fair sample of a book of which the "Lancet " says —"Very sensible advice—terse, interesting, instruc- tive, well considered, and accurate." Don't talk to others of your children's good or bad qualities. . Don't indulge in the impression that everybody else's child is likely to contaminate yours, and that yours CALI contaminate no one's. • Don't expect every One to admire them. Don't tell them that they are clever or that they are stupid. Don't tell them that they came from monkeys, or grew in cucumber beds. Don't niggle, naggle, or haggle them. Don't thrust yourself too much upon them, or let them feel that you are a bore, Don't tease or vex them, and never be unreal towards them. Don't play tricks or pranks with them, or make them jealous. Don't encourage your children to have secrets unknown to you. Don't permit the use of intoxicating liquors or tobacco in any shape or form. tt Scribner's Magazine" for October is an excep- tionally strong number. "The Unpublished Letters of Thackeray," which have proved such delightful reading, are concluding, and they are accompanied by two portraits of the great novelist, and a reproduc- tion of one of his funny sketches. An article on "The Paris School of Fine Arts" has the place of honour, and it is fib ely and atnply illuatrated. We have th e eon- elusion of "The Sacred Flame of Torin Ji," by Mr E. H. House with the illustrations from the charming draw- ings of Mr. G. E. Barnes. Another important illus- trated paper is on " Caverns and Cavern Life," and is from the pen of Mr. N, S. Shaler. Mr. G Brad- ford contributes a paper on " Municipal Government," and Mr. L. Swinburne one on "The Bucolic Dislect of the Plains " ; and there are beside several poems and stories of a high order. The current issue of "The English Illustrated Magazine" has for frontispiece an engraving of a por- trait study by Mr. E. F. Brewtnall, R.W.S., formerly of Warrington. It is an altogether beautiful face. Mr. A. G. Swiiaburne contributes an address " To a Seamew," which is likely to be more popular than many of hie poems. It is exceedingly melodious. " Coaching Days and Coaching Ways," by Mr. W. C. Tristram, starts well. The text is racy, and the drawings by Mr. Hugh Thompson and Mr. Herbert Railton leave nothing to be aesired. "Summer in Somerset:" is another illustrated article, aud there are beside " The Story of Jael," and the National Hymn written for the United States by P. Marion Crawford, &c. We have also to hand part 35 of " Ward and Lock's Technical Journal." Amongst he contents of the cur- rent issue are articles on the student's introduction to mechanics, the grazier, the bricklayer, the 6' eeanaker, the workman as a technical student, B.:c.

div.head: Gni PENHALL AND DARESBURY REVISION COURTS. DEFECTIVE LISTS.
div.p: Gni PENHALL AND DARESBURY REVISION COURTS. DEFECTIVE LISTS.

On Tuesday Mr. C. Lloyd, barrister, held a court at the Barry Arms, Grappenhall, for the purpose of revising the lists for the townships of Grappenhall, Latchford, and Appleton. The Liberals were repre- sented by Mr. T. C. Raynor, and the Conservatives by Mr. L. Bentley and Mr. H. J. Longton. Little of public interest arose in connection with the revi- sion. In regard to the lists for Appleton township considerable trouble was caused by the imperfect manner in which they had been prepared. Mr. Calvert, agistant overseer for the township, was present, but in re- ply to the Revising Barrister be stated that ha had been appointed to the office so recently that be had had nothing to do with the getting out of the lists complained of.—Mr. Raynor remarked that a fine ought to he imposed, and in reply the Revising •Barrister Said that if the person respon- sible had not ceased to hold office he should certainly have been fined unless he had given a very good reason for the state of the lists.—Mr. Bentley: He has submitted to us I lists which are correct, but he has submiited to the Clerk of the Peace fists which are not correct, and which are not pub- lished.-Revising Barrister : Yes ; and tt Is supposed that the lists which are supplied to the Clerk of the Peace are the correct lists. He (the Revising Barrister) had done the best he could with the lists, but tha way the voters' names had te be marked added immensely to the chances that they I might be omitted after all.—Mr. Bentley: It is an ex- I traordinary list, and one which might have caused a great amount of unpleasantness in the division.—The Revising Barrister said that as result o the way in which the lists had been made out about forty persons might have been dis- franchised.—Mr. Raynor suggested that the overseers might be summoned before the Revising Barrietea.—The Revising Banister said that unfortunately that was the last day of hie circuit in that division.—Mr. Bentley: I do not see why you should not summon them to Crewe.--The Revising Bar- rister: I will see about it —Mr.Bentley : And make provis- ion that they should walk all the way there. (Laughter.) —The Revising Barrister thought that would be beyond his jurisdiction. (Laugbter..)—The matter then dropped.—Mr. W. Roberts appeared on belialf of Joseph Hughes, Bold attest, Warrington, who was on the list for property in Wash-lane, Latchford, Mr. Hughes had been objected to by the Conservatives on 4e ground tl'at there was no qua!-, itic :tion stated in the third column of the list.—Mr. Rob- erts said that Mr. Hughes had been on the list for twenty years in respect of this very property.—Mr. Bendy coatene ' tied that there was no qualification stated but ;f the Revis- ing Barrister said he could amend he should not abject. I The Revising Barrister, after some consideration, said he thought it was within his discretion to say whether a mis- take had been made, and be would say that a mistake had been made and amend the statement the qualification. The objection was accordingly disallowed. Mr. Roberts asked for expenses but the Revising Barrister said he did not think it was a case for costs. On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Lloyd also held a court at Deresbury for the'revision of the lists of the townships of Acton Grange, Antrobus, Daresbury, Hatton, Kekewick, Moor, Newton-by-Daresbury, Sevenoaks, Stretton, Walton Inferior, Walton Superior. Whitley, Inferi- or, and Whitley superior. The liberals were again repre- sented by Mr. Raynor and the conservatives by Mr. Bent. ley. There was nothing of imp ortance raised in connection with the revision.

div.p: Pita to the tr,ditor.
FE-B-ERTRORPE DISASTER,

Sir,—Hav-in-gTiarTsome years'experience of railway signal-1 ling and other work in connection with working railway traffic under such circumstances as those which caused the above, I hope I may be allewed to say a few words upon the ver- dict the jury found against the two men Taylor and Davies. Now, from the evidence as gathered from the press, in my opinion they should have been exonerated from all blame, and highly commended for their behaviour; for did Taylor not Stand to his post true as steel and did all be possibly could to avert the accident? But distance would not allow him to do it I effectaally. Let people place themselves in his position. Could they have done more? He displayed great promp- titude and coolness under the circumstances. But it will be asked, why did he run the risk, and why did be disobey the instructions, knowing the block system was suspended? The case is very clear, for when he drew up to the junction why were the borne and starting signals lowered? for they bad mo eght to have been wed at all for anything what- ever, while the block was suspended. Through being lowered, the driver weuld be certain to be under the im- pression that the absolute system was being worked again— and put on full steam accordingly—fur he is bound to run his train to time ; and as to the tligmen, they either did not know how to signal, or they were very negligent in not using detonators, or there was not enough of men out to work the line in safety. For, as was stated when be rounded the carve, be saw the train standing 200 yards away, why was not a man placed to protect the ticket plat- form whether any train was in or not—and also placed at every part where there is a curve? They should be in sight of each other, with a free use of detonating signals, and men that thoroughly understood their duty. If it had been so no accident would have happened. If a line at such times has so much traffic upon it that the ahshlute system of signalling has to be suspended, it can be worked quite safely under very rigid regulations, making each flagman into a section. But it requires men who know what duty they have to perform, and the whole under the superintendence of a thoroughly practical man. No tyamanent signals ought to be used, and so train shoull run at a greater speed than eight miles per hour over the part so worked. Now, Taylor has borne a good character for years as a driver of express trains, and, after due consideration, if he had not used his efforts, the case mieht have been worse. Hie conduct does not seem in any way deliberate reckless- ness but of course be is a poor driver, who may be ruined for life with regard to a situation. The company have got some one to pot the blame upon, but in my opinion it has been placed upon the wrong parties. Tt;anking you for this space, I am, dear sir. AN EX-SIGNALMAN. October sth, 1897.
WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY/

The winter session of this society was opened on Monday evening, when a private Shakesperian re- cital was given in the Public Hal? by Mr. S. Brand- ram. The president of the society for this year, Mr. Robert Davies, of Birch Dale, Stockton Heath, had issued invitations to all the members of the society, to the members of the Warrington Field Club and their wives, and also, amongst others, to the following ladies and gentlemen :—Lady Mary Powys, the Misses Powys, Lady Greenall and the Misses Greenall, the Rev. Canon Greenall, Mrs. Greenall, the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington (Major and Mrs. Pickmere), Mrs. Moreland Crosfield and party, Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Thomas, the Rev. E. Charley and Mrs. Charley (Frodsham), the officers of the Bth and 40th Regimental Districts, Mrs. Braba- zon (Lymm), the Rev. John Yonge, Mrs. Yonge, the Rev. William Brookes, Mr. Gregg (Crown Prosecu- tor, Cork), the students of the Warrington Training College, and the students of the Clergy Daughters' School. In all there were nearly 800 guests. As Mr. Brandram is recognised throughout the country as the Prince of Reciters, it is hardly necessary to say that the performance left little room for criti- cism. His enunciation is at all times clear, his ges- lure graceful, and his modulation of voice almost perfect. The selections from Shakespeare which he gave were of the most varied character, and the fact that Mr. Brandram admirably succeeded in all of them testifies to his extraordinary versatility. In the scene from the "$l, inter's Tale," Autolycus and the Shepherd were presented, by trick of voice and facial expression, as two remarkably distinct characters. The well-known scene between Wol- • sey and Cromwell was powerfully declaimed, with here and there a reading that would be new to many of the audience. Mr. Brandram, apparently with a view to heightening the effect, sometimes gives a rising inflection when a sense seems to , require a falling one. He was not less successful in delineating the strikingly opposite characters of Caliban and Trinculo,in the Tempest," Falstaff was well hit off in Henry IV., but the other characters were less distinctive. The fine qualities of Henry V. were well brought out in his representation of the Warrior King at Agincourt; but it was when Prince Hal played the lover in the scene between the King and Catherine, that Mr. Brandram was, in our judgment, at his best. His rendering of the broken French and English was perfect in its way, and made a capital impression on the audience. Al- together the performance was of a character admir- ably in keeping with the Literary and Philosophi- cal Society, and Mr. Robert Davies, as president, is to be congratulated on a great success in his new and admirable departure.
The programme was as follows : —Winters's Tale, "The sheep sheering," Part of Act 4; Henry VIII., Wolsey and Cromwell; Tempest," Caliban, Trin- culo," part of At 2; King Hal (in three charac-

Continued ease prevails in the money market, and the directors of the Bank of England made no alteration in the rate on Thureday, which remains at 4 per cent. Everybody expected that with the commencement of October business would show marked signs of improvement lon the Stock Exchaege, but with the close of the first week matters terminate in a more depressed state than ever. The past week bee been one of unusual depression, even count- ing the stagnation of previous weeks. There has been one special feature, however, and each week possesses some speci.l characteristic of its own. This week diamond mining shares have had a boom of a very decided character, the diamond trade being forge buyers of shares. The amalgamation of various companies under one working was Vie primary cause of this, and the promise of limited output to send up prices In diamonds counts for the rest. The next boom is most likely to be in Transvaal gold miningAares, as, with the rapid advance at the Dela- gaa Bey Railway, things in the Transvaal are sure to im- prove; and the country, even now almost a terra incognita, will be opened up and its real value recognised. Other markets in the Stock Exchange are almost neglected, foreign stocks showing little variation, the uncertain state of European affairs leaving little room fJr any assurance as to the future. IThe American market is even duller than the English, and if only a little life were pat into thing, on the other s'cle there is not e uch room to doubt that they would re- ceive support here. In the present condition of things the stagnation is due to the absence of the public, who continue' to hold aloof. The public are "bulls," and, believing the time unpropitious. keep off, had they been " bears." they would have made a lot of money, but the public are seldom "bears." A subject which claims an important interest to a large section of the public, is building societies, which are re- garded at the present time in Many circles as being ?Isar a crisis. A recent return shows there are 1,848 of these societies in the United Kingdom, of these 446 ex- hibit deficits amounting in the aggregate to £161,183. The proposed reconstruction of La Triaadad, Silver Queen, and the rest of the Abbott Page group is engaging the attention of various interests. Shareholders in these com- panies have virtually lost everything, and the proposal to subscribe a further £240,000 would appear utterly ridiculoas were it not interests involved of such a magni- tude that every effort will be made to induce shareholders to approve of the proposal. The chief subscribers, it need hardly be said, are in the country, and, if they were willing, it is more than doubtful whether they would be able to pay the heavy burden it is intended to put upon them. The original promoters of those schemes are out of the , reckoning. Mr. J. Neill, of Abbott, Page, and Co., is gone. Mr. J. T. Browne, the vendor, admits his inability to meet the claims upon him, and the shareholders of La Trinadad have therefore only the directors to look to, and they should certainly be made responsible for the statements in the prospectus.

GREAT SCANDAL AT RUNCORN.

A TRADESMAN INVOLVED. Within the past week a tradesman respectably connected, and very popularly known in Runcorn, has not put in his appearance at his usual haunts, and yesterday the rumours and conjectures that were indulged in assumed a more definite shape. Although a benedict of many years, with a family growing up around him, he was looked upon by his associates as - a "Gay Lothario.' His visits to the seaport city were neither few nor far between, and a reason for his numerous ex- cursions is now supplied. One wife of his bosom was not; it seems, sufficient, and in secret, it is stated, he espoused a second helpmate. Two years have elapsed since this violation of the British law took place, but only within a few brief hours of this publication has there been any revelation of the circumstance. There is every appearance of truth about the story told that under an assumed name he sought and won the love of a guileless maiden, and unable to accomplish his base designs in any other manner he led the girl to the alter. Thus for the period of time mentioned he has led a double life, and his guilt has been screened by the fact that he represented himself as the traveller of a firm with a well-known name in the town, and with the provi- sion attached that he should reside in Cheater. Runcorn, however, has been his habitation during the day, and he has spent his eveningB with his second charmer. It is said that he has never missed spending the Sunday with her since the nuptial knot was tied.' Already the misguided girl has become a mother, and there is reason to believe will soon have a se- cond arrow added to her quiver, The parents have obtained a knowledge of the true facts of the case; and there will soon be a hue and cry for the base seducer on the serious charge of " bigamy." The difficulty, it is expected, will be to find the missing man.

div.head: RE-OPENJNG OF HOLY TRINIIY CHURCH.
div.p: RE-OPENJNG OF HOLY TRINIIY CHURCH.

Yesterday, Holy Trinity Church, Warrington, Was re-opened after undergoing repairs which will add considerably to the comfort of the congregation, and to the appearance of the interior of the build- ing. Holy Communion was celebrated at eight o'olock in the morning; there was a shortened morning prayer and sermon by the Bishop of Liverpool at noon; and in the evening there was evening prayer and sermon by the Rev. T. B. Armit- stead, 8.A., vicar of Winmarleigh. The offerings at the mid-day service were in aid of the restora- tion fund, and at the other services they were in aid of she expenses of the wardens, whose funds have suffered from the necessary closing of the church for a term of nearly three months. The services are 'to be continued to-mor- row (Sunday), when the Vicar will preach in he morning, and the Rev. S. J. T. Darwall in • the evening. The mid-day service yesterday was con- ducted by the Vicar (the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton), and the following surpliced clergymen were pre- sent: Canon Whitley, the Revs. S. Wilkinson (St. Paul's), G. D. Wray (St. Peter's), W. H. Williams (Padgate), I. Philips (Orford), T. B. Ariaitstead ffinmarleigh), and IV. E, Glenn. In the course of his sermon Bishop Ryle said that the more simple, and the more plainly understood, every part of public worship was, the more like it was to the New Testament standard. Everyone of a congregation should take a part, and the sing- ing should not be left to the choir, and the res- ponses to the parson and the clerk. -Those who put the people aside, and made them mere spectators, made a great mistake. The people Were intended to be a part of the whole business, and to join clearly in prayer and praise. The whole benefit of public worship de- pended upon the spirit 'and the, manner in which that worship was made. It should be made with deep reverence, and to public worship they should take with them their hearts, and their voices too. They were just now called upon to do something to wipe off the debt remaining on the restoration of the church. He remembered coming to the church the first day that he was the Bishop of Liverpool, and thinking that there was great room for im- provement. That improvement had taken place, and he congratulated the ministers and congrega- tion of Holy Trinity on the change. In conclusion he said that he understood that something like £5O was required, antl he urged his hearers to give liberally.

div.head: ALDERMAN HARRISON AND DALLAM
div.p: ALDERMAN HARRISON AND DALLAM
FORGE WORKMEN.
The following is a copy of correspondence which has taken place respecting some remarks recently made at the Warrington Police Court by Alderman Harrison ;

Bedford Hotel Company, Limited, Brighton, 1 Oct., 1887. Dear Alderman Harrison,—Some one has sent to me a "Warrington Guardian" containing remarks by you, from the bench, which it seems to me were uncalled for, and which / am sure were unjust. That we, should be careless of the character of the men who work for us, is in itself extremely un- likely, and as a matter of fact is not true; bad men are not often good workmen; dishonest men,, drunken men, and disorderly men, are not willingly admitted into workshops, but men who may not have had the advantage of much education and training must yet earn their living, and as they "do not wear their heart upon their sleeve for daws to peck at," their employers cannot always tell what their faults are, and whether they are. such as should exclude them from their service. In— even magistrates—are faulty and fallible persons, and when we have found a fact and passed a sen- tence, we may well spare gratuitous observa- tions founded upon no evidence. The Pear- son and Knowles Company were not before the court; they endeavour to do their duty all round, and they do not expect their workmen to be better than the ordinary men of their own class, and they are very confident they are not- worse. Ido not like to make any nubile •nt upon what passes in a police court. I give every one credit for desiring to act fairly and squarely, but you must excuse my saying that the Bench is not privileged (like Parliament) to makeirrelevant and injurious observations respecting any one— especially any one not before it.—Yours faithfully, H. BLECIELY.

S, Woodbine Terrace, Latchford, 2nd October, /887. Dear Mr. Bleckly,—ln reply to your favour re- ceived this morning, I am bound to confess that the remarks made by me at the Borough Court, to which you refer, and of which You justly complain, were very unfortunate, inasmuch as they conveyed a very different meaning to that which I intended. They were quite unpremeditated and uttered in the warmth of the moment, and provoked, I may say, by the irritating conduct of Mr. Percy Davies. I assure rat nothing could have been further from my intention than to have uttered a Word cal- culated to have wounded the susceptibilities either of the employers or the employed of your justly eminent firm.

Mr. Percy Davies, at the court before referred to, persistently repeated three or four times, that be- cause the man (charged with a very brutal assault upon his wife) had worked at the "Dallam Forge," on and off for 15 years, he could not have been guilty of the repeated acts of cruelty, drunkenness, and general had conduct with which she charged him, and this argument he used to discredit the poor woman and her witnesses. This appeared to me to be so absurd and weak in the face of the evi- dence against his client, that it provoked my re- joinder, by which I simply meant "How can the Dallam Forge Co., or any other large employers of labour, be expected to know, and if they did know, to control the moral characters of such men as the accused outside the works, so long as they do the work efficiently for which they are paid." But as a matter of fact, the firm of "Pearson, Knowles, and C 0.," was never mentioned, nor did it ever occur to me at the time, that it and the "Dallam Forge Co," were convertible terms; therefore I could not have had any premeditated intention of offering an affront either to the one or the other. My allusion was meant to apply generally to any large employers of labour.

However, I do net seek shelter under any mere technicality. I must admit that I have (though un- intentionally) done a wrong for which I am very sorry, and only too anxious to make all the repara- tion in my power, and as the offensive remark is taken to apply to the eminent firm of which you are one of the leading spirits, I can only take one plain and obvious course, from which no honourable man should shrink, viz., to express my unqualified regret. that I should have been betrayed into do- ing so, and lam sanguine enough to hope that you will generously accept this avowal of my error, as my " amende honorahle,"—Believing you will do so, I remain, yours very faithfully, J. IlAnuisobr. Henry Bleckly, Esq., J.P.
